objectives.title: Think Like an Economist
objectives.body: Use incentives, opportunity cost and marginal thinking to frame a business decision.

objectives.title: Read Official Data
objectives.body: Find, read and question CBN, NBS, IMF and FRED data — levels, rates of change, breaks and revisions.

objectives.title: Build a Macro Dashboard
objectives.body: Choose the few numbers your board should watch and present them clearly every month.

figures.title: Headline, Food and Core Inflation
points: Headline inflation covers everything in the basket; food is about half of a Nigerian household budget.
Core removes volatile farm produce and energy — a better guide to underlying pressure.
Inflation climbed from about 22% to 34% after the mid-2023 reforms.
In January 2025 the CPI was rebased: the sudden drop is partly a change of yardstick, not only a change in prices.

figures.title: Two Prices for One Dollar
points: For years the official rate and the parallel market rate differed — at times by more than 100%.
A big premium is a signal of rationing: dollars are scarce at the official price.
Firms that could not access official dollars paid the parallel price — and priced their goods off it.
After the 2023–24 unification the gap almost closed, at a much weaker naira.

figures.title: Strong Correlations Can Mislead
points: Credit growth and inflation move closely together (r = 0.82) — but both jumped after the 2023 devaluation, which revalued dollar loans and raised prices.
The oil price and reserves have a weak correlation (r = 0.31), yet the causal channel is clear: oil earnings supply most of Nigeria's dollars.
Correlation strength tells you how tightly two series move, not whether one causes the other.
Ask: is there a third factor, a time lag, or reverse causation?

figures.title: Did Savers Beat Inflation?
points: Real rate = policy rate − inflation.
For most of 2015–2024 it was negative: money in the bank lost purchasing power.
Negative real rates push savers into dollars, property and stocks — and weaken the naira.
In 2025 the real rate turned clearly positive, helped by rate hikes — and by the CPI rebasing.

figures.title: The PMI as a Nowcast
points: The Purchasing Managers' Index asks firms whether output, orders and employment are up or down.
It is published within days of the month's end.
Shaded periods: the PMI dropped below 50 in every downturn.
Use it alongside your own sales data, not instead of it.

figures.title: Six Numbers on One Page
points: Each panel: latest value, the trend over three years and the change on a year ago.
Inflation, policy rate, exchange rate, oil price, reserves and PMI cover prices, money, the currency and activity.
Same layout every month, so directors see change at a glance.
Add one line of 'so what' under each number for your business.

items: Economics is a management tool: incentives, opportunity cost and marginal thinking frame every decision.
Always separate nominal from real and naira from dollars.
Know your sources, and check for rebasing, revisions and multiple rates.
Correlation is not causation: look for third factors, lags and reverse causation.
A good board dashboard is short, consistent and tied to a 'so what'.
recap.prework: Re-read the Note on Microeconomics for Managers, sections on demand, supply and elasticity. Bring one price your company changed in the last year and what happened to volumes.

glossary.def: The value of the best alternative you give up.
The extra benefit or cost of one more unit.
Measured in current prices, including inflation.
Adjusted for inflation; shows volume or purchasing power.
Year-on-year change in the full consumer price index.
Inflation excluding volatile items such as farm produce and energy.
Updating the base year and basket of an index; breaks comparisons.
Gap between the parallel and official exchange rates.
Nominal interest rate minus inflation.
Estimating current activity from fast, timely signals.

lab.title: Lab: Build the Board's Macro Page
steps: Load the data and look at the latest three months before calculating anything.
Build a table of six indicators: latest value, value a year ago, and the change.
Add two derived numbers: the real policy rate and the FX premium.
Compare inflation before and after the CPI rebasing.
Write one 'so what' line for your own company under each number.
lab.deliver: a one-page dashboard with six numbers and six 'so what' lines for your board.

hook.title: Five Numbers Before Breakfast
hook.quote: “Our sales are up 30% this year. The board is delighted.”

concepts.title: Taking Inflation Out of the Numbers
concepts.plain: A nominal number is measured in today's naira. A real number strips out inflation so you can see whether volumes or purchasing power really changed.
concepts.formula: real growth ≈ nominal growth − inflation
concepts.example: Sales up 30% while prices rose 28% → real growth of roughly 2%. The business barely grew.
concepts.why: Bonuses, targets and investment cases set in nominal naira reward inflation, not performance. Always ask for the real number.

concepts.title: Seeing the Economy Before GDP Is Published
concepts.plain: GDP arrives months late. Nowcasting uses faster signals — surveys, payments, fuel sales, electricity use — to estimate what is happening now.
concepts.formula: PMI > 50 → activity expanding;  PMI < 50 → contracting
concepts.example: The PMI fell below 50 in 2016, during COVID-19 and again in the 2024 reform squeeze — each time before GDP data confirmed the slowdown.
concepts.why: Your own data are nowcasting signals too: daily sales, distributor orders and collections often tell you about the economy weeks before the statistics office does.

checks.q: Your division's naira revenue grew 30% last year while inflation averaged 28% and the naira lost half its dollar value. What is the best summary?
options: Strong growth — 30% beats most competitors
Revenue roughly flat in real terms, and down sharply in dollars
Revenue fell 28% in real terms
We cannot say anything without profit data
checks.explain: B. Real growth ≈ 30% − 28% ≈ 2%, so volumes barely moved. In dollars, 1.30 × 0.5 = 0.65, a 35% fall. A ignores inflation; C misapplies the formula; D is too cautious — revenue alone tells us a lot.

checks.q: Inflation on the dashboard fell from 34.5% to 16.4% in a year, but the CPI was rebased in January 2025. What should the CFO tell the board?
options: Inflation has halved — we can cut prices
Part of the fall reflects the new base and basket, so we should watch month-on-month changes and core inflation before acting
The rebasing makes all inflation data useless
Ignore inflation and watch the exchange rate only
checks.explain: B. A change of base year and basket changes the measured rate. Month-on-month changes and core inflation on the new basis give a cleaner read. A over-reacts; C and D throw away useful information.

case.title: The Board's Macro Page
case.context: A Lagos FMCG company imports a third of its inputs and sells only in naira. Its board meets monthly and receives forty pages of numbers.
case.question: Which five or six macro numbers should the directors see every month — and how should they be shown?
case.data: ng_macro_monthly.csv — 132 months (2015–2025) of inflation, policy rate, exchange rates, oil price, reserves, money, credit and PMI. *Stylised teaching data.*
case.decision: A one-page dashboard: each number with its latest value, change on a year ago and a one-line 'so what' for the business.

objectives.title: Read a Market
objectives.body: Use demand and supply to explain why a price moved, and predict who bears a cost increase.

objectives.title: Measure Elasticity
objectives.body: Estimate own-price, cross-price and income elasticities from sales data — holding other things constant.

objectives.title: Price Under Uncertainty
objectives.body: Decide how much of a cost shock to pass on, using elasticity, rivals' behaviour and customers' reference prices.

figures.title: Who Pays When Flour Gets Dearer?
points: Higher flour costs shift the supply curve up: firms need a higher price to supply the same quantity.
The new equilibrium has a higher price (+10%) and a lower quantity (−13%) in this example.
The price rises by less than the cost: part of the shock is paid by customers, part by producers.
How it splits depends on elasticity: the less sensitive the buyers, the more they pay.

figures.title: Prices Tripled — Volumes Did Not Collapse
points: Lagos shelf price went from about ₦162 to ₦518 a pack between 2022 and 2025.
Volumes rose in the North and Lagos, and fell in the South-East.
Looks like customers do not care about price. Do not believe it yet.
Incomes, competitors' prices and the general price level all moved at the same time.

figures.title: Inflation Hides the Elasticity
points: Plotting units against shelf price gives an elasticity of just −0.09 — 'price barely matters'.
But every price was rising: competitors' prices, wages, the whole price level.
What matters to a shopper is our price relative to the alternatives and to their income.
To see the true response we must hold the other drivers constant.

figures.title: What Customers Really Respond To
points: Own price −1.47: a 1% rise in our price, all else equal, cuts volume by about 1.5%.
Cross price +0.73: when a rival raises its price by 1%, we gain about 0.7% volume — they are close substitutes.
Income +1.11: as customers' incomes rise, they buy more.
Method: one regression of log(units) on log(own price), log(rival price), log(income), a time trend and region.

figures.title: When Does a Price Rise Pay?
points: With elasticity −0.5, a 20% price rise raises revenue.
At our estimate (−1.47), a 20% rise cuts revenue by about 8%.
But revenue is not profit: if the price rise covers higher costs, it can still protect margin.
Elasticity is lower when all firms raise prices together — the market is less elastic than a single brand.

figures.title: Big Jumps Hurt More Than the Arithmetic Says
points: We compared actual sales with what the elasticity model predicts.
Promotion weeks (price below usual) sold about 4% more than predicted.
Prices up to 5% above usual: no extra penalty. More than 10% above: −7.7%.
The penalty fades as the new price becomes the new 'normal' — reference prices adapt over weeks.

figures.title: What a 15% Discount Buys
points: Promotion weeks (15% off) sold 32–36% more packs than normal weeks.
Part of that is genuinely new demand; part is pantry loading — customers buying earlier, not more.
Measure the weeks after a promotion too: a dip means you borrowed sales from the future.
Promotions also reset reference prices downward if they run too often.

figures.title: How Much of the Flour Shock to Pass On?
points: The shock adds ₦63 to a pack that sells for ₦500 and costs ₦350 to make.
Absorb it all: volume holds, but profit falls to 58% of what it was.
Pass it all on, rivals holding: volume −16%, profit back to 84%. If rivals follow: volume −8%, profit 92%.
Since all millers face the same flour price, rivals are likely to follow — so passing on most of it, in steps, is the stronger option.

items: Prices come from demand and supply; a cost shock shifts supply and is shared between buyers and sellers.
Separate a move along a curve from a shift of the curve.
Measure elasticity holding other things constant — inflation hides it.
Own, cross and income elasticities tell you how volume reacts to you, rivals and the economy.
Customers judge prices against a reference price: stagger, explain and time increases.
recap.prework: Read Sahay, Time Series Analysis and Forecasting (BEP8370), the chapters on trend and seasonality. Bring one demand number your company forecasts every year and how far off last year's forecast was.

glossary.def: How much buyers want at each price, all else equal.
How much sellers offer at each price, all else equal.
The price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.
Price changes move along a curve; other drivers shift it.
% change in quantity for a 1% change in own price.
% change in our quantity for a 1% change in a rival's price.
% change in quantity for a 1% change in income.
The price a shopper expects, based on recent experience.
Losses feel worse than equal-sized gains feel good.
Share of a cost change that ends up in the selling price.

lab.title: Lab: How Price-Sensitive Are Our Customers?
steps: Look at prices and volumes by region from 2022 to 2025.
Estimate the naive elasticity (units on price only) and explain why it misleads.
Estimate own-price, cross-price and income elasticities holding other things constant.
Compute the volume and revenue effect of 5%, 10% and 20% price rises.
Test pass-through of 0%, 50% and 100% of the flour shock — with rivals holding and following.
lab.deliver: a 3-sentence pricing recommendation to the MD: how much to pass on, how fast, and what to watch.

hook.title: Flour Is Up 40%. What Do We Charge?
hook.quote: “Our flour bill has jumped 40%. Just add it to the price — customers have no choice, everybody eats noodles.”

concepts.title: Own-Price Elasticity of Demand
concepts.plain: Elasticity tells you by what percentage volume changes when price changes by 1%. If the number is bigger than 1 (ignoring the minus sign), demand is elastic: customers react strongly. Smaller than 1 is inelastic.
concepts.formula: elasticity = % change in quantity ÷ % change in price
concepts.example: Our noodles: elasticity ≈ −1.47. A 10% price rise loses about 13% of volume when rivals hold their prices.
concepts.why: Elastic demand means a price rise reduces revenue; inelastic demand means it raises revenue. Knowing which one you face is the start of every pricing decision.

concepts.title: Reference Prices and Loss Aversion
concepts.plain: Shoppers judge a price against the price they are used to — their reference price. Paying more than usual feels like a loss, and people weigh losses about twice as heavily as equal gains.
concepts.formula: pain of a ₦50 rise  >  pleasure of a ₦50 cut
concepts.example: Weeks priced more than 10% above the usual price sold about 7.7% fewer packs than the elasticity alone predicts.
concepts.why: Several small, explained increases usually cost less volume than one big jump. Pack-size changes ('shrinkflation'), clear communication and timing all manage the reference price.

concepts.title: Dynamic Pricing — Power and Limits
concepts.plain: Dynamic pricing changes prices often, using data on demand, stock, time and competitors. Ride-hailing surge pricing and airline fares are examples. AI makes it cheap to estimate elasticities by product, store and hour.
concepts.formula: price ↑ when demand is high or capacity is scarce
concepts.example: A ride-hailing app raises fares in Lagos rush hour and during heavy rain, when many riders compete for few drivers.
concepts.why: It can raise revenue and balance supply and demand, but it can also feel unfair and invite regulators. Rules of thumb: be transparent, cap surges on essentials, and never personalise prices in ways customers would object to.

checks.q: A competitor cuts its noodle price by 10%. Our cross-price elasticity is +0.73. Holding our price, what happens to our volume?
options: Rises about 7%
Falls about 7%
Falls about 15%
No change — cross-price only matters for complements
checks.explain: B. Cross-price elasticity +0.73 means a 1% change in the rival's price moves our volume 0.73% in the **same** direction. A 10% cut by them → about 7% fewer packs for us. C uses the own-price elasticity; D has substitutes and complements the wrong way round.

checks.q: Flour costs rise 40% for every noodles maker in Nigeria. Which statement is most accurate?
options: We should absorb the cost; any price rise loses customers to rivals
Rivals face the same shock, so the relevant elasticity is closer to the market's (less elastic) — passing on most of the cost in steps is likely to protect profit
Pass on exactly 40% because flour rose 40%
Price does not matter; the naive elasticity is close to zero
checks.explain: B. When all firms face the same cost, they tend to move together and the volume loss is smaller (own + cross ≈ −0.74). A ignores rivals' costs; C confuses the flour rise with the unit-cost rise (only 45% of cost is flour); D is the inflation trap.

case.title: Pricing Noodles Through a Flour Shock
case.context: A Nigerian noodles maker sells a single-serve pack in three regions — Lagos, the North and the South-East. Shelf prices have more than tripled since 2022 as costs and the exchange rate moved.
case.question: Flour, about 45% of unit cost, has just risen 40%. How much of the extra cost should be passed into price, and how fast?
case.data: fmcg_price_volume.csv — 209 weeks × 3 regions: shelf price, competitor price, promotion weeks, an income index and packs sold. *Stylised teaching data.*
case.decision: A pricing recommendation that uses measured elasticities, a view on rivals' response and the risk of breaking customers' reference price.

objectives.title: Read a Demand Series
objectives.body: Separate trend, seasonality and one-off shocks in monthly sales data.

objectives.title: Forecast and Test
objectives.body: Build a simple trend-plus-season forecast, backtest it against rules of thumb, and express it as a range.

objectives.title: Size a Market
objectives.body: Estimate a Nigerian market top-down and bottom-up, and reconcile the two.

figures.title: Ten Years of Cement Demand
points: National consumption grew from 18.7 million tonnes in 2012 to 32.2 million in 2025 — about 4.3% a year.
The 12-month moving average smooths out the seasons and shows the trend.
Three shocks: the 2016 recession, the 2020 lockdown and the 2024 price spike.
Each time, demand recovered to the trend within about a year.

figures.title: The Rainy Season Rhythm
points: February is about 14% above an average month; July and August about 18% below.
Rain stops site work, so demand dips from June to September.
Plan capacity, stock and cash for the peak months, not the annual average.
Schedule maintenance shutdowns for the rainy season, when demand is lowest.

figures.title: Pretend It Is January 2024
points: We fitted each method on 2012–2023 only and asked it to forecast 2024–2025.
Then we compared the forecasts with what actually happened.
This is a backtest: the only honest way to judge a forecasting method.
The model followed both the season and the trend; 'same month last year' missed the growth.

figures.title: Which Method Forecast Best?
points: Trend + seasonal model: 4.1% average error — the best.
'Same month last year': 5.8%. The common budget rule 'last year + 5%': 6.6%.
A flat average ignores the seasons: 10.9% error.
MAPE = mean absolute percentage error: on average, how far off were we?

figures.title: 2026: A Number and a Range
points: Base forecast for 2026: about 32.9 million tonnes.
Monthly bands show where each month will probably fall (90% range).
For the year: roughly 31.0–34.9 million tonnes, based on how far past years strayed from the model.
Say it as a range: 'about 33, very likely between 31 and 35'.

figures.title: Plan for More Than One Future
points: Downside (−8%): another cement price spike and weak real incomes → 30.3 mt.
Base: trend and season continue → 32.9 mt.
Upside (+6%): a large housing and road programme → 34.9 mt.
Ask: what capacity is safe in the downside and expandable in the upside?

figures.title: More Complex Is Not More Accurate
points: We made the trend curve more and more flexible.
Fit to the past barely changed (about 4% error).
Forecasts of the future got much worse: from 4% to over 90% error at the most flexible.
This is overfitting: the model memorises the past instead of learning its pattern.

figures.title: Do the Two Routes Agree?
points: Top-down: 32.2 mt. Bottom-up: 33.8 mt. Within about 5% — reassuring.
If they disagree badly, one of the assumptions is wrong. Find it before you build.
New homes are the biggest segment: watch mortgage rates, real incomes and land policy.
Both estimates sit close to the time-series forecast — three independent views pointing the same way.

items: Demand = trend × season × shocks; read each part separately.
A transparent trend-plus-season model beats most budget rules — backtest to prove it.
Always give a range and scenarios, not a single number.
More complex is not more accurate: judge models on unseen data.
Size markets top-down and bottom-up, and reconcile the two.
recap.prework: Read the Ant Financial case (917-0029-1). Come ready to say: is Ant a bank, a technology company or a marketplace — and why does the answer matter for regulators?

glossary.def: The long-run direction of a series.
A pattern that repeats at the same time every year.
A month's typical level relative to an average month (100).
An average of the last N periods; smooths out noise and seasons.
Testing a forecasting method on past data it was not built on.
Mean absolute percentage error: the average size of forecast misses.
The band within which the outcome will probably fall.
A coherent story of the future with its own numbers.
A model that memorises past noise and forecasts badly.
Sizing from the whole economy vs adding up the uses.

lab.title: Lab: Cement Demand in 2026
steps: Compute annual totals and the average growth rate since 2012.
Compute the seasonal index: each month versus its year's average.
Fit a trend + seasonal model on 2012–2023.
Backtest it on 2024–2025 against 'same month last year' and 'last year + 5%'.
Forecast 2026, and compare with the top-down and bottom-up market sizes.
lab.deliver: a two-sentence 2026 capacity recommendation: how many tonnes, and what flexibility you keep.

hook.title: A ₦100 Billion Bet on One Number
hook.quote: “Demand grows 5% every year. Build the new line — we'll sell everything we make.”

concepts.title: Trend × Season: A Forecast in One Line
concepts.plain: Our forecast says: next month's demand = the trend level for that month × the seasonal index for that calendar month. We fit both from history with one regression.
concepts.formula: forecast = trend(t) × season(month)
concepts.example: Trend level for August 2026 ≈ 2.76 mt; August index ≈ 0.82 → forecast ≈ 2.26 mt.
concepts.why: Simple models are transparent: a manager can see and challenge every assumption. That matters more than an extra decimal of accuracy.

concepts.title: Start From the Whole Economy
concepts.plain: Top-down sizing starts from a big, known number — population, GDP, households — and multiplies by a rate of use per person or per naira.
concepts.formula: market = population × use per person
concepts.example: 230 million people × about 140 kg of cement each per year ≈ 32.2 million tonnes.
concepts.why: Quick and easy to sanity-check against other countries. But the 'use per person' assumption carries all the weight — and it differs widely between countries at similar income levels.

concepts.title: Add Up the Uses
concepts.plain: Bottom-up sizing builds the market from its parts: how many homes, roads, factories and repairs, times the cement each one needs.
concepts.formula: market = Σ (units of activity × cement per unit)
concepts.example: About 450,000 new homes × ~32 tonnes = 14.4 mt, plus repairs (6.5), public works (6.0), commercial (4.5), precast (2.4) = 33.8 mt.
concepts.why: Slower, but it shows which segments drive demand — and which ones a new government programme or a price shock would hit.

checks.q: Your sales team forecasts next year as 'this year + 10%'. A trend-plus-seasonal model forecasts +4%, with a range of −2% to +10%. What should you do?
options: Use +10% — the sales team knows the market
Use +4% and ignore the sales team
Start from the model's +4% and ask the sales team for named, specific reasons for any upward adjustment; plan capacity for the range
Average the two: +7%
checks.explain: C. The model is the disciplined baseline; judgement should adjust it only for specific, recorded reasons (a new contract, a new region). D splits the difference without evidence. And capacity should be planned against the range, not a point.

checks.q: Top-down sizing gives 32 million tonnes; bottom-up gives 45 million tonnes. What is the best next step?
options: Average them: 38.5 mt
Trust the bottom-up figure because it is more detailed
Find which assumption explains the gap (e.g. tonnes per house or homes built) and check it against independent data
Use whichever supports the investment case
checks.explain: C. A large gap is information: one of the inputs is wrong. Detail does not make bottom-up right — 13 extra million tonnes usually means an inflated activity count or usage rate. D is how bad investments get approved.

case.title: How Much Cement Will Nigeria Buy?
case.context: A Nigerian cement company is deciding whether to add a new production line for 2026. Demand has grown for a decade, but it dipped in the 2016 recession, during COVID-19 and in the 2024 price spike.
case.question: How many tonnes of cement will Nigeria consume in 2026 — and how confident can we be?
case.data: cement_demand_monthly.csv — 168 months (2012–2025) of national cement consumption, price per bag, a rainy-season flag and a building-permits index. *Stylised teaching data.*
case.decision: A 2026 forecast with a range and scenarios, checked against an independent market-sizing estimate.

objectives.title: Classify a Market
objectives.body: Place an industry on the spectrum from perfect competition to monopoly, and say what that means for prices and profits.

objectives.title: Understand Platforms
objectives.body: Explain two-sided markets, network effects, switching costs and data as sources of market power.

objectives.title: Think Like a Regulator
objectives.body: Measure concentration (CR and HHI), and judge when a dominant firm or a merger becomes a competition problem.

figures.title: What Market Power Costs Society
points: Under competition, price falls to the cost of the last unit, and output is high.
A monopolist restricts output to push the price up.
Gold area: value transferred from customers to the monopolist.
Red area: deadweight loss — purchases worth more than they cost that simply never happen.

figures.title: From Banks to Platforms
points: In 2016 banks' apps and USSD handled 78% of mobile-payment value.
By 2025: banks 28%, KoboLink 30%, SwiftNaira 19%, AgentPay 11%.
Fintechs won by going where banks were weak: agents in markets, cheap POS, simple apps.
The market became more competitive between banks and fintechs — and more concentrated among fintechs.

figures.title: Concentration Depends on How You Define the Market
points: Treat 'banks' as one block: HHI falls from 6,222 to 2,238 — the market looks ever more competitive.
Treat them as ~10 separate banks: HHI rises from 746 to 1,532 — concentration is growing.
Same data, opposite stories. Defining the market is the first and most contested step in any competition case.
Ask: who do customers actually switch to when one provider raises its price?

figures.title: Users and Merchants Grew Together
points: Active users rose from 12 million to 97 million; merchants from 0.3 million to 7.3 million.
Each 1% more users came with about 1.6% more merchants.
The two sides reinforce each other: more users attract merchants, who attract more users.
This feedback loop is why platform markets can grow very fast — and tip towards a leader.

figures.title: Winner-Takes-Most Among the Fintechs
points: Within the fintech segment, KoboLink went from 15% to 45% of payment value.
PayFast, the early leader, fell from 46% to 9%.
Being first is not enough: the platform that builds the network fastest wins.
Once a network tips, rivals need a big advantage — or regulation — to catch up.

figures.title: Fees After Dominance
points: KoboLink entered cheaper than rivals: about 0.50% of value, against roughly 0.69% for others.
As its share passed a quarter of the market, its fee rose to about 0.54%.
Still below rivals — so customers are not obviously harmed yet.
A regulator would watch the trend, merchant complaints, and whether rivals can still win business.

items: Market structure runs from perfect competition to monopoly; most markets sit in between.
Market power raises prices, cuts output and creates deadweight loss.
Measure concentration with CR and HHI — but define the market first.
Platforms grow through network effects, switching costs and data — and can tip.
Regulators judge conduct, not size; interoperability keeps markets open.
recap.prework: Read 'Externalities: Justification for Public Goods?' (210-023-1) and the UVA note on pollution taxes and cap-and-trade. Think about one cost your industry imposes on others that it does not pay for.

glossary.def: Ability to raise price above cost without losing most customers.
A market dominated by a few large, interdependent sellers.
Value lost because worthwhile trades do not happen.
Combined share of the largest firms, e.g. CR2.
Sum of squared market shares; 0 to 10,000.
A platform serving two groups who value each other.
A product becomes more valuable as more people use it.
The cost or hassle of moving to a rival.
When a network market swings decisively to one leader.
Rules that let rival networks connect and exchange.

lab.title: Lab: Is the Payments Market Competitive?
steps: Tabulate market shares by provider and year.
Compute CR2 and the HHI for each year.
Recompute the HHI treating 'Banks' as ten separate banks — compare the two stories.
Measure two-sided growth: % more merchants per 1% more users.
Check whether the leader's fee rises with its share; test the SwiftNaira–AgentPay merger.
lab.deliver: a 3-sentence note to the competition regulator on the proposed merger.

hook.title: Is the Biggest App Too Big?
hook.quote: “Five years ago nobody had heard of them. Now every market woman in Lagos has their POS — and their fees just went up.”

concepts.title: The Herfindahl–Hirschman Index (HHI)
concepts.plain: The HHI adds up the squared market shares of every firm. Squaring gives big firms more weight. A pure monopoly scores 10,000; many tiny firms score close to 0.
concepts.formula: HHI = s₁² + s₂² + … + sₙ²   (shares in %)
concepts.example: Four firms with 40%, 30%, 20%, 10%: 1,600 + 900 + 400 + 100 = 3,000 — highly concentrated.
concepts.why: Competition authorities use the HHI to screen mergers. A merger's effect on the index is roughly 2 × s₁ × s₂ — two firms of 15% and 10% add 300 points.

concepts.title: A Platform Serves Two Groups at Once
concepts.plain: A platform connects two groups who need each other: payers and merchants, riders and drivers, buyers and sellers. Each side values the platform more when the other side is bigger.
concepts.formula: value to a user ↑ as merchants ↑   and   value to a merchant ↑ as users ↑
concepts.example: A trader accepts KoboLink because many customers pay with it; customers download it because many traders accept it.
concepts.why: Platforms often subsidise one side (free app for users, free POS for agents) to win the other. Low prices today can be a strategy, not a gift.

concepts.title: When a Platform Becomes a Bank
concepts.plain: Ant Financial (now Ant Group) grew from Alipay, a payments tool, into lending, wealth management and insurance for hundreds of millions of Chinese users — using payments data to score credit.
concepts.formula: payments → data → credit → more payments
concepts.example: In 2020 Chinese regulators halted Ant's planned stock-market listing and required it to restructure under bank-style rules.
concepts.why: Nigerian fintechs follow a similar path from payments to lending. The case asks: should a platform that behaves like a bank be regulated like a bank?

checks.q: A market has five firms with shares 30%, 25%, 20%, 15% and 10%. What is the HHI?
checks.explain: B. 900 + 625 + 400 + 225 + 100 = 2,250. A sums the shares; C is a guess; D would need a single firm with 100%. 2,250 sits in the 'moderately concentrated' band of the US 2010 guidelines.

checks.q: SwiftNaira (19%) and AgentPay (11%) want to merge. Using HHI ≈ 1,532 before the deal, what does the merger do?
options: Raises the HHI by about 30 points — no concern
Raises the HHI by about 418 points, taking it to about 1,950 — the deal deserves close review
Lowers the HHI because the merged firm can compete with KoboLink
Has no effect: HHI only changes when firms enter or exit
checks.explain: B. ΔHHI = 2 × 19 × 11 = 418, moving the market into the moderately concentrated band. The merged firm *might* challenge KoboLink (C's argument) — that is a defence the parties would make, but the index itself goes up.

case.title: Nigeria's Mobile-Payments Market
case.context: Between 2016 and 2025, the share of payment value handled by banks' own apps and USSD fell from 78% to 28%. Fintech platforms — agents, POS terminals and apps — took the rest. One platform, 'KoboLink', now handles 30%.
case.question: Is a dominant payments platform good for customers (scale, convenience, low cost) or a competition problem (lock-in, higher fees, blocked rivals)?
case.data: payments_market_shares.csv — 10 years × 6 providers: share of payment value, active users, merchants and average fee. *Stylised; providers other than the banks are fictional.*
case.decision: A reasoned view for the regulator: how concentrated the market is, whether fees signal market power, and what — if anything — should be done.

objectives.title: Diagnose a Market Failure
objectives.body: Recognise externalities, public goods, asymmetric information and market power in your own industry.

objectives.title: Choose the Right Fix
objectives.body: Compare Pigouvian taxes, cap-and-trade, regulation, nudges and market design — and when each works.

objectives.title: Analyse a Subsidy
objectives.body: Work out who really gains from a subsidy, who loses when it goes, and what compensation should look like.

figures.title: The Generator Next Door
points: The generator owner pays for fuel and maintenance — the private cost.
Neighbours pay too, in noise, fumes and health — the external cost.
The market uses generators up to where private cost meets benefit: too much.
A tax equal to the external cost moves use to what is best for society — the idea behind a Pigouvian tax.

figures.title: Most of the Money Went to the Better-Off
points: The richest 10% of households received about 37% of the household petrol subsidy.
The poorest 40% received only about 9%.
In naira, the richest households got about 38 times as much as the poorest.
This pattern — subsidies captured by the better-off — is found in fuel subsidies across many countries.

figures.title: Naira Received vs Share of Budget
points: Bars: the subsidy in naira rose steeply with income.
Line: as a % of the budget, it also rose — from about 3% for the poorest to 12% for the richest.
Poor households mostly use petrol indirectly: through bus fares and the cost of moving food.
That indirect channel is why removal still hurt the poor badly.

figures.title: The Cost of Removal
points: Direct cost: petrol rose from ₦185 to ₦617 a litre.
Indirect cost (our assumptions): bus fares +50%, food +10%.
Extra cost: about 14% of the budget for the poorest decile, 23% for the richest.
For the poor, most of the hit is indirect — and they have the least room to cut back.

figures.title: Targeted vs Universal Support
points: A ₦10,000 a month transfer to the poorest 40% leaves the poorest two deciles better off than before removal.
The same budget spread over everyone gives just ₦4,000 each — too little to protect the poor.
Better-off households still bear the full cost — but they also gained most from the subsidy.
Targeting needs a reliable social register, digital IDs and payment channels.

figures.title: What the Savings Can Buy
points: The household petrol subsidy cost about ₦6.7 trillion a year (stylised).
The targeted transfer costs about ₦2.1 trillion — roughly 31% of that.
The rest can fund transport (e.g. CNG buses), health and education — or cut borrowing.
Credibility matters: people accept reform more readily when they can see where the savings go.

items: Markets fail through externalities, public goods, information gaps and market power.
Fix them by pricing the harm (taxes, permits), rules, nudges or market design.
Governments fail too: compare imperfect alternatives.
A per-litre subsidy goes to whoever uses the most — usually the better-off.
Protect the poor with targeted transfers, and show where the savings go.
recap.prework: Read the chapters on aggregate demand and aggregate supply in Blanchard, Macroeconomics. Bring one price your company raised in 2024 and say whether the cause was demand (customers buying more) or supply (your costs rising).

glossary.def: When a free market produces the wrong amount of something.
A cost or benefit that falls on people outside the transaction.
Non-excludable and non-rival, so markets under-supply it.
Enjoying a benefit without paying towards it.
One side of a deal knows more than the other.
A tax equal to the external cost of an activity.
A fixed total of pollution permits that firms can trade.
A change in defaults or framing that steers choices.
Who actually bears a tax or receives a subsidy.
When intervention makes outcomes worse.

lab.title: Lab: Subsidy Incidence and Compensation
steps: Compute the subsidy each decile received, in naira and as a % of budget.
Find the shares of the richest 10% and the poorest 40%.
Estimate the direct and indirect cost of removal; change the fare and food assumptions.
Cost a targeted cash transfer and compare it with the old subsidy bill.
Find the transfer that leaves deciles 3 and 4 no worse off.
lab.deliver: a two-sentence recommendation on how the savings should be used.

hook.title: Who Really Got Cheap Petrol?
hook.quote: “The petrol subsidy was the one benefit ordinary Nigerians got from the oil wealth.”

concepts.title: The Lemons Problem
concepts.plain: When buyers cannot tell good from bad, they pay an average price. Owners of good products then refuse to sell, the average quality falls, and the market can unravel.
concepts.formula: hidden quality → average price → good sellers leave
concepts.example: Lenders cannot tell safe from risky small businesses, so they charge everyone high rates — which drives away the safest borrowers first. Credit bureaus and collateral registries exist to fix this.
concepts.why: Your business can profit from solving information problems: warranties, ratings, certification, track records, and data-based credit scoring all build trust.

concepts.title: Pigouvian Taxes vs Cap-and-Trade
concepts.plain: A tax fixes the price of pollution and lets the quantity adjust. Cap-and-trade fixes the quantity and lets the price adjust. Both make polluting costly, so firms that can cut cheaply do the most cutting.
concepts.formula: tax: price fixed, quantity varies  ·  cap: quantity fixed, price varies
concepts.example: A gas-flaring penalty per thousand cubic feet is a tax-style tool; a carbon market with a national emissions cap is the permit approach. Session 13 returns to carbon pricing.
concepts.why: For your business: either tool turns pollution into a cost line. Firms that cut emissions early gain a cost advantage — or permits to sell.

concepts.title: Interventions Can Fail Too
concepts.plain: Governments face their own problems: poor information, lobbying by those who benefit, leakage and corruption, and policies that are easy to start but hard to stop.
concepts.formula: market failure ≠ automatic case for intervention
concepts.example: The petrol subsidy was meant to share oil wealth, but it favoured car and generator owners, encouraged smuggling across borders, and became one of the largest items in the federal budget.
concepts.why: The right question is not 'market or government?' but 'which imperfect arrangement does least harm here?'

concepts.title: Who Really Benefits From a Subsidy?
concepts.plain: A per-litre subsidy goes to whoever buys the most litres. Rich households use far more petrol — for cars and generators — so they receive far more in naira, even if the subsidy is a bigger share of a poor family's budget.
concepts.formula: benefit = litres used × subsidy per litre
concepts.example: Before removal (stylised): ₦315 of subsidy per litre. A household in the richest 10% using 150 litres a month got ₦47,250; one in the poorest 10% using 4 litres got ₦1,260.
concepts.why: Universal price subsidies are an expensive way to help the poor. Most of the money goes to people who do not need it.

checks.q: A Lagos estate's residents all run diesel generators, and everyone complains about the noise and fumes. Which policy best fits the economics of externalities?
options: Ban generators outright
Charge a fee per generator-hour that reflects the harm, and use the money to co-fund a shared, cleaner power supply
Do nothing — residents chose to live there
Subsidise diesel so generators are cheaper to run
checks.explain: B prices the externality (a Pigouvian charge) and funds an alternative. A is costly when there is no grid power; C ignores a real cost imposed on others; D makes the over-use worse.

checks.q: Our data show the richest 10% got 37% of the subsidy but face the largest % cost from removal (23% of budget vs 14% for the poorest). What follows?
options: Removal was regressive because the rich lost more
The rich lose more in % terms, but they gained most from the subsidy and can absorb it; protecting the poorest — who have little margin — is the priority for compensation
Compensation should go mainly to the richest decile
The subsidy should be restored
checks.explain: B. The burden as a % of budget is only part of the story: the poorest are closest to subsistence, and they received least from the subsidy. A misuses 'regressive'; C and D ignore who benefited and the fiscal cost.

case.title: Petrol Subsidy Removal
case.context: For decades Nigeria held the pump price of petrol below its cost, paying the difference from public funds. In mid-2023 the subsidy was removed and the pump price rose from about ₦185 to ₦617 per litre.
case.question: Who gained from the subsidy, who loses from its removal, and what should replace it?
case.data: fuel_subsidy_incidence.csv — household spending, petrol use, food and transport shares, vehicle and generator ownership, by consumption decile. *Stylised teaching data.*
case.decision: A policy recommendation: how the savings should be used, and how to protect poor households at a sensible fiscal cost.

objectives.title: Use the AD–AS Model
objectives.body: Tell a demand shock from a supply shock, and predict what each does to prices and output.

objectives.title: Read Inflation Measures
objectives.body: Explain headline, food, core and trimmed-mean inflation, and why each answers a different question.

objectives.title: Respect Expectations
objectives.body: Explain why inflation is sticky, and why central banks care so much about what people expect.

figures.title: Demand Shock vs Supply Shock
points: Demand shock: spending jumps → prices and output rise together. Overheating.
Supply shock: costs jump → prices rise but output falls. Stagflation.
Both raise inflation, so inflation alone cannot tell you which happened.
Look at output and activity too: are firms selling more, or less?

figures.title: Food Running Ahead of Core
points: Food inflation exceeded core inflation almost every month.
The gap averaged +5.3 points over 2015–2024 and widened to about +12 points in 2024.
Food prices react to fuel, transport, insecurity and the exchange rate — mostly supply forces.
A wide food–core gap is a warning that interest rates alone will not fix the problem.

figures.title: Exchange-Rate Pass-Through
points: When the naira weakens, imported goods and inputs cost more in naira.
In this data the link is strongest about 2 months later (correlation 0.84).
The naira's fall after mid-2023 was the single largest cost shock for many firms.
Pass-through is a supply shock to importers — but a weaker naira also helps exporters.

figures.title: Prices Up, Activity Stalled
points: Each dot is one month: PMI (activity) against inflation.
In 2015–19 inflation averaged 13.3% with the PMI around 50.7.
In 2023–24 inflation averaged 28.7% while the PMI averaged only 50.0.
Inflation more than doubled without a boom in activity — consistent with a supply shock.

figures.title: Taking Out the Extremes
points: This illustrative month: petrol and vegetables jumped; data and electricity barely moved.
The weighted mean (headline) is 3.2% — pulled up by two big movers.
Drop the top and bottom 15% of the basket by weight: the trimmed mean is 2.6%.
When the two diverge, a few items are driving headline inflation — often a supply story.

figures.title: Inflation Is Sticky
points: Each dot compares inflation now with inflation 12 months earlier.
The fitted line: inflation now ≈ 0.74 + 1.13 × last year's rate.
A slope near or above 1 means high inflation tends to stay high — or rise further.
Why? Contracts, rents, wages and prices are set looking backward and forward.

figures.title: Expectations Shift the Curve
points: The Phillips curve links inflation to slack: less spare capacity, more pressure on prices.
But each curve is drawn for a given level of expected inflation.
If people come to expect 30%, the curve shifts up: the same slack now comes with 30%-type inflation.
So central banks fight hard to keep expectations anchored — even at the cost of growth.

items: AD–AS: demand shocks move prices and output together; supply shocks move them apart.
Diagnose before you prescribe: rates cure demand inflation far better than supply inflation.
Use headline for the cost of living; core and trimmed mean for the underlying trend.
Watch for rebasing — a new ruler is not a new reality.
Inflation is sticky because of expectations; credibility is worth fighting for.
recap.prework: Read the Mankiw chapters on measuring national income (GDP). Find your company's revenue for the last three years and ask: how much of the growth was real?

glossary.def: Total spending on an economy's goods and services.
Total output firms will produce at each price level.
A change in spending that moves prices and output the same way.
A change in costs that moves prices and output in opposite ways.
High inflation combined with weak or falling output.
Inflation excluding volatile items such as farm produce and energy.
Average price change after dropping the most extreme movers.
How much of an exchange-rate change shows up in local prices.
The link between economic slack and inflation.
People's belief that inflation will return to target.

lab.title: Lab: Diagnose the 2023–24 Inflation Surge
steps: Compare headline, food, core and PMI before and after mid-2023.
Compute the food minus core gap by year.
Correlate inflation with naira depreciation at different lags — where is the link strongest?
Fit inflation now against inflation a year ago to measure persistence.
Check the real policy rate: were rates above or below inflation?
lab.deliver: a three-sentence diagnosis — demand, supply or both — citing at least two numbers, and one implication for your pricing.

hook.title: From 22% to 34% in Eighteen Months
hook.quote: “Prices are rising because people have too much money. Raise interest rates and it will stop.”

concepts.title: The Same Medicine Does Not Cure Both
concepts.plain: Higher interest rates work on demand: they make borrowing dearer and cool spending. Against a supply shock they cannot bring fuel or dollars back — they mainly reduce output further, while stopping the shock from spreading into wages and expectations.
concepts.formula: demand shock: P↑ Y↑   ·   supply shock: P↑ Y↓
concepts.example: Mid-2023 to end-2024, average inflation was 30.5% against 19.6% in the eighteen months before, while the PMI slipped from 52.7 to 49.4. Prices up, activity down: the supply-shock signature.
concepts.why: If you misdiagnose a supply shock as demand, you expect rate rises to fix prices quickly. They won't — so plan for costs that stay high and customers who spend less.

concepts.title: Rebasing Changes the Ruler
concepts.plain: A price index compares today's basket with a base year. When statisticians rebase, they update the base year and the basket weights. Year-on-year rates before and after are not directly comparable.
concepts.formula: inflation = (CPIₜ ÷ CPIₜ₋₁₂ − 1) × 100
concepts.example: Nigeria's CPI was rebased in January 2025. In this dataset headline inflation drops from about 34% in December 2024 to about 24% in January 2025 — much of that is the new ruler, not a sudden collapse in price pressure.
concepts.why: Before you change prices, wage offers or contract indexation clauses, check which index and which base year the number uses.

checks.q: A sudden rise in diesel and imported-input costs pushes Nigerian prices up while factories cut output. In AD–AS terms this is:
options: A rightward shift of aggregate demand
An upward (leftward) shift of aggregate supply
A movement along aggregate demand caused by higher incomes
A fall in aggregate demand caused by lower prices
checks.explain: B. Higher production costs shift AS up and to the left: prices rise and output falls. A would raise output, not cut it. C and D describe demand, which is not where this shock started.

checks.q: Headline inflation is 30%, core is 22% and the trimmed mean is 23%. What is the best reading?
options: Underlying inflation is about 30%, so plan for 30% every year
A few items (likely food and energy) are pushing headline above the underlying trend of about 22–23%
Core inflation is wrong because it leaves out food
Inflation is under control because core is lower
checks.explain: B. When core and trimmed mean agree and sit well below headline, a small group of volatile items is driving headline. Those items still hurt households (so C is a fair complaint, but not the best reading), and 22% is far from 'under control' (D).

case.title: Demand Problem, Supply Problem — or Both?
case.context: After the May–June 2023 reforms, Nigerian inflation climbed from about 22% to the mid-30s by 2024. The CBN raised its policy rate sharply. Firms faced rising costs and weakening customers at the same time.
case.question: Was the surge mainly a demand shock (too much spending) or a supply shock (costs pushed up)? The answer decides whether higher interest rates are the right medicine.
case.data: ng_macro_monthly.csv — headline, food and core inflation, exchange rates, policy rate and PMI, 2015–2025. *Stylised teaching data.* We use 2015–2024 for like-for-like comparisons because the CPI was rebased in 2025.
case.decision: A short diagnosis with evidence (food vs core, exchange-rate pass-through, activity), and what it implies for policy and for your pricing.

objectives.title: Read the National Accounts
objectives.body: Explain GDP, GDI and GNI, nominal versus real, and what a rebasing does — and does not — change.

objectives.title: Find the Growth Drivers
objectives.body: Separate oil from non-oil growth and spot which sectors are gaining share.

objectives.title: Judge Living Standards
objectives.body: Use per-person, PPP and 'beyond GDP' measures to size a market honestly.

figures.title: Nominal vs Real GDP
points: The gold line is GDP in current naira; the navy line removes inflation.
From 2010 to 2025 nominal GDP rose 6.8×; real GDP rose 1.51×.
The widening gap after 2022 reflects the inflation surge you saw in Session 6.
Plan capacity on real growth; plan cash and prices on nominal.

figures.title: Same Economy, Bigger Measured GDP
points: Rebasing updates the base year, the sector weights and the coverage of new activities.
Here the rebased series is about 36% higher in every year — an illustrative uplift.
Growth rates change much less than levels.
Ratios to GDP (debt, tax, credit) all fall at once — read them with care.

figures.title: Who Contributes to Growth?
points: Bars split each year's growth into non-oil (teal) and oil & gas (gold).
Non-oil activity provided almost all the growth; oil subtracted in most years from 2012 to 2023.
In 2022 oil output fell about 19% in this data while non-oil grew 4.8%.
Oil is small in GDP but huge for dollars and government revenue — that is why it still moves the naira.

figures.title: The Changing Shape of the Economy
points: ICT & telecom roughly doubled its share, from 7.5% to 15.8% of real GDP.
Oil & gas fell from 15.8% to 5.7%.
Agriculture and trade remain the largest sectors, at about a quarter and a sixth of output.
Manufacturing stayed near 6.5% — little sign of industrialisation.

figures.title: Bigger Economy, Same Average Income
points: Real GDP rose to 151 (2010 = 100); population rose to 147.
Real GDP per person ended at only 103 — almost no gain in fifteen years.
Population grows about 2.6% a year; GDP must beat that just to stand still.
For consumer businesses: more customers, but not richer ones. Volume and value strategies differ.

figures.title: How Long to Double Living Standards?
points: Years to double ≈ 70 ÷ growth rate.
At 3% per person, income doubles in about 23 years; at 7%, about 10.
At this data's 0.2% per person, it takes about 376 years.
Small differences in growth, compounded, decide whether a generation gets richer.

figures.title: Market Rates vs PPP
points: At market exchange rates, GDP per person here is about $1,100; at PPP about $6,300.
PPP adjusts for the fact that haircuts, food and rent cost less in Lagos than in London.
Nigeria's PPP-to-market ratio (5.7×) is the highest in this group — partly because the naira fell so far.
Use PPP to compare living standards; use market rates to price imports or report in dollars.

figures.title: The Economy the Statistics Struggle to See
points: Informal firms are unregistered and often unseen by surveys and tax.
In this data Nigeria's informal share is about 57% of GDP — the highest of the group.
Across countries, richer economies are less informal: about 1.5 points less per $1k of PPP income.
For managers: much of your market is cash-based, informal and hard to size — triangulate with your own sales data.

items: GDP can be measured by output, spending or income; Nigeria's GNI is below its GDP.
Always separate nominal from real; the deflator tells you how much was inflation.
Rebasing changes levels and ratios, not what the economy did.
Non-oil sectors drive growth, but oil still drives dollars and revenue.
What matters for customers is income per person — and here it has barely moved.
recap.prework: Read the HBS Note on Money and Monetary Policy (9-797-076) and the CBN brief on liquidity management. Note how your company's borrowing rate changed between 2023 and 2025.

glossary.def: Value of all final goods and services produced in a country in a period.
Output minus the inputs bought from other firms.
GDP plus net income received from abroad.
GDP at constant prices: shows changes in volume.
Nominal ÷ real GDP × 100: the broadest price index.
Updating the base year, weights and coverage of the accounts.
Exchange rate that equalises what money can buy across countries.
Activity that is unregistered and largely unmeasured.
Output per worker or per hour; the root of living standards.
Years to double ≈ 70 ÷ the annual growth rate.

lab.title: Lab: Is Nigeria Getting Richer?
steps: Compute real GDP growth year by year.
Split growth into oil and non-oil.
Rank sectors by average annual growth, 2010–2025.
Compute real GDP per person and the years it would take to double.
Compare market-rate and PPP income across peers.
lab.deliver: a short paragraph for the board: real growth, growth per person, and the two sectors that matter most for your demand.

hook.title: Bigger Overnight — Richer Overnight?
hook.quote: “Nigeria is now Africa's largest economy.” — headlines, April 2014

concepts.title: Taking Prices Out of GDP
concepts.plain: Nominal GDP values output at today's prices; real GDP values it at a fixed base year's prices, so it moves only when quantities move. The ratio of the two is the GDP deflator — the broadest price index we have.
concepts.formula: deflator = nominal GDP ÷ real GDP × 100
concepts.example: In this data nominal GDP rose 6.8× from 2010 to 2025, real GDP only 1.51×. Most of the 'growth' in naira was inflation; the deflator rose about 30% in 2024 alone.
concepts.why: A market that grows 25% in naira while prices rise 30% is shrinking in volume. Always ask for real growth before celebrating.

checks.q: After a rebasing, Nigeria's measured GDP rises 36% while the debt stock is unchanged. Which statement is right?
options: The government can now borrow 36% more safely
Debt-to-GDP falls, but the government's ability to pay — its revenue — has not changed
Living standards rose 36%
Real growth last year was 36%
checks.explain: B. The denominator grew, so the ratio falls, but debt is paid from revenue, not from GDP. Nothing about incomes (C) or last year's growth rate (D) changed; borrowing capacity (A) depends on revenue and interest costs.

checks.q: Real GDP grows 3.4% and population grows 2.6%. Roughly how fast is real income per person growing, and how long until it doubles?
options: 3.4% a year; about 20 years
About 0.8% a year; about 90 years
6.0% a year; about 12 years
It cannot be calculated without PPP data
checks.explain: B. Per-person growth ≈ 3.4% − 2.6% = 0.8%. Using the rule of 70: 70 ÷ 0.8 ≈ 88 years. A ignores population; C adds instead of subtracts; D is wrong — PPP is not needed for a growth rate.

case.title: Is Nigeria Getting Richer?
case.context: A consumer-goods company plans its five-year strategy. The CEO's slide says 'Nigeria's economy has grown 50% since 2010'. The CFO is less sure the average customer is better off.
case.question: How much has the economy really grown, which sectors are driving it, and has income per person risen enough to grow our market?
case.data: ng_gdp_sectors.csv — real GDP by ten sectors (₦ tn, 2010 prices), nominal GDP on old and new bases, population, 2010–2025; peer_income.csv — ten countries. *Stylised teaching data.*
case.decision: A one-paragraph view for the board on real growth, growth per person, and the sectors that matter for our demand.

objectives.title: Explain the Toolkit
objectives.body: Describe what a central bank targets and how it uses the policy rate, reserves, open-market operations and its balance sheet (QE and QT).

objectives.title: Trace Transmission
objectives.body: Follow a rate decision through banks, markets, the exchange rate and expectations to prices and output — and explain the lags.

objectives.title: Judge the Stance
objectives.body: Use real rates, liquidity conditions and a simple rule to judge whether policy is tight or loose.

figures.title: A Worldwide Tightening Cycle
points: Most central banks cut to near zero in 2020 and kept rates there through 2021.
In 2022–23 the US Fed, ECB and Bank of England raised rates at the fastest pace in decades.
Higher US rates pulled dollars out of frontier markets like Nigeria and Ghana.
From 2024–25 the rich-country banks began to cut; Nigeria stayed high.

figures.title: Size of the Hiking Cycles
points: From their post-COVID lows to their peaks: Ghana +16.5, Nigeria +16.0, Kenya +6.0 points.
The US Fed raised by 5.25 points, from 0.25% to 5.5%.
African banks hiked more because inflation and currency pressure were far higher.
Bigger hikes also had to compensate investors for currency risk.

figures.title: Rates, Inflation and the Interbank Market
points: For most of 2020–2023 the MPR stayed below inflation — a negative real rate.
The 2024 hikes closed much of the gap; in 2025 the real rate turned clearly positive (helped by the CPI rebasing).
The interbank rate (teal) is what banks actually pay each other — it does not always follow the MPR.
Judge policy by the real rate and the interbank rate, not the headline MPR alone.

figures.title: When the Policy Rate Does Not Bind
points: When banks are flush with naira, interbank rates fall far below the MPR — down to −9.5 points in late 2020.
Then a 'high' MPR does little: money is cheap anyway.
In 2024 the CBN drained liquidity and interbank rates rose above the MPR (up to about +5.4 points).
That is when tightening really started to bite.

figures.title: Did Tight Policy Slow Money and Credit?
points: Credit growth peaked at about 61% (Dec 2023) and broad money at about 63% (Jun 2024).
Much of that was revaluation: dollar loans and deposits were worth more naira after devaluation.
As revaluation faded and policy tightened, growth fell to about 9% (credit) and 19% (M2) by end-2025.
Lesson: in a devaluation, naira money and credit numbers overstate real expansion.

figures.title: The Rate Gap and the Naira
points: The teal line is the gap between the CBN rate and the US Fed rate — what a dollar investor earns for holding naira.
The dashed line is how much the naira then fell over the next 12 months.
In 2022–23 the naira fell far more than the gap — investors lost money, so they stayed away.
Once the gap exceeded expected depreciation in 2024–25, portfolio inflows returned.

figures.title: Was Policy Tight Enough?
points: The gold line is the illustrative rule; navy is the actual MPR.
The MPR sat below the rule in about 85% of months, 2015–2024.
The gap was widest in 2023–24, at the height of the inflation surge.
Use the rule to ask 'how tight?', not to forecast the next MPC decision.

items: Central banks control the price of money; they use rates, reserves, OMO and their balance sheet.
QE and QT abroad change the cost of dollars for Nigeria.
Policy works through banks, markets, the naira and expectations — with long lags.
Judge the stance by real and interbank rates, not the headline MPR alone.
Fiscal dominance undermines credibility and raises everyone's borrowing costs.
recap.prework: Read 'Net Fiscal Operations' and the CBN brief on the Fiscal Responsibility Law. Find what share of federal revenue went on interest in the latest budget.

glossary.def: The CBN's benchmark rate signalling the price of money.
The rate banks charge each other for overnight naira.
Share of deposits banks must hold at the CBN.
Central-bank sales or purchases of securities to manage liquidity.
Central-bank asset purchases with newly created money.
Shrinking the central bank's balance sheet.
The chain from a policy decision to prices and output.
Policy rate minus inflation.
A formula for where the policy rate 'should' be.
When government finance needs override inflation control.

lab.title: Lab: How Fast Does the Rate Reach Your Firm?
steps: List every CBN policy-rate decision and its size.
Compute the real policy rate by year.
Compare the interbank rate with the MPR to judge liquidity.
Correlate rate changes with credit growth at different lags — and ask why correlation misleads here.
Compute an illustrative Taylor-rule rate and compare it with the MPR.
lab.deliver: a short note for your CFO on funding costs, customer demand and the naira over the next 12–18 months.

hook.title: Nearly Nine Points in Ten Months
hook.quote: “The MPC voted to raise the Monetary Policy Rate by 400 basis points to 22.75%.” — CBN, February 2024

concepts.title: When the Rate Hits Zero: The Balance Sheet
concepts.plain: Quantitative easing (QE): the central bank creates money to buy government bonds and other assets, pushing long-term rates down. Quantitative tightening (QT) is the reverse: it lets those bonds mature or sells them, draining money and pushing long rates up.
concepts.formula: QE: CB buys bonds → reserves ↑, long yields ↓   ·   QT: reverse
concepts.example: The US Fed's balance sheet grew to almost $9 trillion by 2022, then began shrinking under QT from mid-2022. Global dollar liquidity tightened just as Nigeria needed dollars most.
concepts.why: QE and QT in Washington change the cost and availability of dollars for Nigerian firms, banks and the government — through Eurobond yields and portfolio flows.

concepts.title: The Taylor Rule
concepts.plain: John Taylor proposed that a central bank should set its rate at a neutral level plus inflation, then add more when inflation is above target or the economy is running hot. It is a yardstick, not a law.
concepts.formula: rate = r* + π + 0.5(π − target) + 0.5 × output gap
concepts.example: With inflation at 34.5%, a 9% target, a 2% neutral real rate and a flat PMI, the rule gives about 49% in December 2024 — far above the actual 27.5%.
concepts.why: The rule shows policy was loose by textbook standards. But against a supply shock, following it mechanically would crush output; the CBN chose to tighten hard but not that hard.

checks.q: The CBN raises the cash reserve requirement while leaving the MPR unchanged. What is the most likely immediate effect?
options: Banks have more money to lend, so loan rates fall
Banks have less naira to lend or place in the interbank market, so liquidity tightens and short-term rates rise
The naira weakens because the CBN is printing money
Nothing — only the MPR matters
checks.explain: B. A higher CRR locks more deposits at the CBN, so banks have less to lend — a tightening even with an unchanged MPR. A is the opposite; C confuses tightening with easing; D ignores the other tools.

checks.q: Inflation is 30%, the MPR is 27.5% and the interbank rate is 31%. Which statement best describes the stance?
options: Very loose: the MPR is below inflation
Roughly neutral to tight in practice: the rate banks actually pay is above inflation, though the MPR itself is slightly below
Very tight: the MPR is above 25%
Impossible to judge without the Taylor rule
checks.explain: B. The interbank rate — the marginal cost of money — is above inflation, so conditions are tighter than the MPR alone suggests. A and C each look at one number only; D overstates the role of the rule.

case.title: How Fast Does the CBN Reach Your Firm?
case.context: In 2024 the CBN raised its policy rate sharply to fight inflation of over 30%, tightened bank reserves and mopped up liquidity. Inflation stayed high for months. Firms asked whether the medicine was working.
case.question: Through which channels does a rate rise reach a Nigerian firm, how long does it take, and was policy actually tight?
case.data: ng_macro_monthly.csv — policy rate, interbank rate, inflation, money, credit, exchange rate and PMI, 2015–2025; global_policy_rates.csv — seven central banks, 2019–2025. *Stylised teaching data.*
case.decision: A short note for your CFO: what the 2024–25 rate path means for funding costs, customer demand and the naira over the next 12–18 months.

objectives.title: Read a Budget Like an Analyst
objectives.body: Separate revenue, primary spending and interest, and judge the burden against revenue as well as GDP.

objectives.title: Use the Debt-Dynamics Equation
objectives.body: Explain why debt/GDP rises or falls using r, g and the primary balance — and spot the 'other' items.

objectives.title: Turn Fiscal Risk Into Business Risk
objectives.body: Link subsidy reform, tax reform, borrowing and sovereign risk to rates, the naira and demand in your market.

figures.title: Moderate Debt, Very Low Revenue
points: Public debt rose from 14% of GDP in 2010 to 42% in 2025 in our stylised data.
FGN revenue stayed around 3–5% of GDP — among the lowest ratios in the world for a large economy.
A debt ratio that is comfortable for a country collecting 20–30% of GDP is heavy for one collecting 5%.
So judge the debt against what the state can collect, not only against the size of the economy.

figures.title: How Much Revenue Goes on Interest?
points: In 2010 interest took about 16 kobo of every naira of federal revenue.
By 2021 it took 93 kobo, leaving almost nothing for salaries, roads or schools without more borrowing.
Higher oil receipts and reforms lowered the ratio to about 67% in 2025 — still very high.
Published reports showed a similar pattern; our numbers are stylised.

figures.title: Years of Revenue Needed to Repay the Debt
points: Debt ÷ revenue: how many years of all federal revenue would repay the stock of debt.
It rose from about 2.5 years in 2010 to a peak of 10.6 years in 2024.
By 2025 it eased to 8.6 years as naira revenue rose faster than debt.
This is the number that explains why investors demand high yields on FGN debt.

figures.title: Revenue: Bigger in Naira, Still Oil-Heavy
points: Oil supplied about 70% of federal revenue in the early 2010s; under 40% in recent years.
Naira revenue jumped after 2022 — partly because a weaker naira raises the naira value of oil sales.
Oil prices and output still swing the budget, so fiscal risk is also commodity risk.
The 2025 tax reform laws aim to raise non-oil revenue; firms should expect tighter tax administration.

figures.title: Inflation Has Been the Debt Ratio's Friend
points: g (nominal growth) includes inflation; r is the average interest rate the state pays.
In most years in our data g exceeded r, so the interest–growth term pulled the ratio down.
When inflation falls, g falls quickly; r falls only as old debt is refinanced.
Lesson: disinflation without fiscal reform can make the debt arithmetic worse.

figures.title: Why Did Debt/GDP Jump in 2023–24?
points: 2023: debt/GDP rose 18.7 points — almost all of it (17.9) in 'other'.
That reflects the CBN overdraft ('Ways and Means') converted into bonds and the naira revaluation of dollar debt.
2024: 'other' added 12.2 points while fast nominal growth subtracted 6.1.
Deficits matter, but the big jumps came from off-budget items and the exchange rate.

figures.title: A Ten-Year Projection
points: Reform (g 20%, r 13%, surplus 0.5%): debt falls to about 19% of GDP by 2035.
Baseline (g 17%, r 15%, deficit 1%): roughly flat at 45%.
Adverse (g 14%, r 17%, deficit 2%, an FX shock in 2027): debt more than doubles to 87%.
The difference comes from assumptions a CFO can watch: inflation, yields, the deficit and the naira.

items: Judge debt against revenue and interest, not only GDP.
Debt dynamics: r − g and the primary balance drive the ratio; 'other' items cause the jumps.
Inflation and devaluation cut both ways: they raise naira revenue and naira-valued dollar debt.
Fiscal stress reaches firms through banks, yields, the naira and demand.
Watch the few numbers that decide the path: yields, inflation, the deficit and the exchange rate.
recap.prework: Read the Silicon Valley Bank case (F-0997-E). Ask your treasury team how much of your bank's or company's investments are in long-dated FGN bonds, and at what yield they were bought.

glossary.def: Revenue minus all spending except interest.
Total spending (including interest) minus revenue.
Public debt as a share of the economy's annual output.
Share of government revenue spent on interest.
Interest rate on debt minus nominal growth; drives the debt ratio.
Changes in debt not explained by the deficit (FX, bailouts, conversions).
Change in GDP per naira of extra government spending.

Central-bank overdraft to the government.
Extra yield investors demand on a country's debt over a safe benchmark.

lab.title: Lab: Is the Debt the Problem — or the Revenue?
steps: Compute debt/GDP, debt/revenue and interest/revenue for every year.
Compute r (interest ÷ last year's debt) and g (nominal GDP growth). In which years was g > r?
Decompose each year's change in debt/GDP into r − g, primary balance and 'other'.
Project debt/GDP to 2035 under a baseline and a reform scenario.
Find the debt-stabilising primary balance for three combinations of r and g.

hook.title: Low Debt, Heavy Burden
hook.quote: “Nigeria's debt is only about 40% of GDP — Japan's is over 200%. What is the fuss about?”

concepts.title: What Moves the Debt Ratio?
concepts.plain: The debt ratio rises when the interest rate (r) on debt is higher than the economy's nominal growth (g), and when the government runs a primary deficit. Anything else — a devaluation, a bailout, an old overdraft turned into bonds — shows up as 'other'.
concepts.formula: Δd = (r − g) ÷ (1 + g) × d  −  pb  +  other
concepts.example: In 2025 in our data: r = 8.3%, g = 23.3%. With g far above r, the interest–growth term cut the debt ratio by about 6 points on its own.
concepts.why: High inflation raises g and quietly erodes the debt ratio — but it also raises future interest rates. The relief lasts only while r stays below g.

concepts.title: Does Government Spending Grow the Economy?
concepts.plain: A fiscal multiplier tells you how much GDP changes when government spending changes by ₦1. It is larger when the economy has idle capacity and smaller when spending leaks into imports or pushes up interest rates.
concepts.formula: multiplier = ΔGDP ÷ ΔG
concepts.example: If ₦1 trillion of road spending raises GDP by ₦0.6 trillion, the multiplier is 0.6. Open, import-dependent economies with high interest rates tend to have multipliers below 1.
concepts.why: When government cuts spending, your demand falls by more in sectors that sell to the state (construction, contractors) and less in export or consumer-staples sectors. Know where your revenue sits.

checks.q: Country A has debt of 40% of GDP and revenue of 5% of GDP. Country B has debt of 80% of GDP and revenue of 35% of GDP. Which is more stretched, and why?
options: Country B — its debt ratio is twice as high
Country A — its debt equals 8 years of revenue versus about 2.3 years in B
They are equally stretched
Neither — debt ratios below 100% are always safe
checks.explain: B. Debt is repaid from revenue. A's debt is 40 ÷ 5 = 8 years of revenue; B's is 80 ÷ 35 ≈ 2.3 years. Debt/GDP alone (A) misleads; there is no universally safe threshold (D).

checks.q: Inflation falls sharply, so nominal GDP growth drops from 23% to 13%, while the average interest rate on government debt stays at 15%. Holding the primary balance constant, what happens to the debt ratio?
options: It falls, because lower inflation is good news
It starts rising, because r is now above g
Nothing — inflation does not affect debt
It falls, because interest rates will fall immediately
checks.explain: B. With r (15%) above g (13%), the interest–growth term turns positive and the ratio drifts up unless the primary balance improves. Rates on existing debt adjust only slowly as bonds are refinanced (D).

case.title: Is the Debt the Problem — or the Revenue?
case.context: Federal debt rose sharply after 2022 as the CBN overdraft was converted into bonds and the naira fell. Interest payments now take most of federal revenue, and banks hold large amounts of FGN bonds.
case.question: Is Nigeria's fiscal problem too much debt, or too little revenue — and what does each answer imply for interest rates, the naira and your company's plans?

objectives.title: Read the Yield Curve
objectives.body: Explain what the level and slope of the FGN yield curve say about inflation, policy and the cost of long-term money.

objectives.title: Spot Interest-Rate Risk
objectives.body: Use duration to estimate how much a bond or a bank loses when rates rise.

objectives.title: Link Stability to Your Firm
objectives.body: Explain how bank fragility and macroprudential rules change credit availability, spreads and investment.

figures.title: From Steep and Low to High and Inverted
points: 2021: cheap short-term money, long rates well above short — a normal, steep curve.
Mid-2024: the CBN's tightening pushed short rates above long rates — an inverted curve.
End-2025: lower and flatter as inflation eased and rate-cut expectations built.
For a CFO the level is the cost of funds; the slope hints at whether to lock in long or stay short.

figures.title: Long Bonds Fall Most
points: All four bonds pay a 13% coupon and are priced at 100 when the yield is 13%.
At an 18.8% yield the 1-year bond barely moves; the 10-year bond falls to about 74.
The 20-year bond falls further still.
Rule of thumb: more duration = more interest-rate risk.

figures.title: What Happened to Bonds Bought in January 2023
points: Take bonds bought at par in January 2023 and value them in June 2024.
Short bonds lost about 5%; 10- and 15-year bonds lost about 20%.
No default, no missed coupon — the loss comes purely from higher market yields.
If you must sell before maturity, that loss becomes real.

figures.title: Long Bonds Funded by Short Deposits
points: Assets ₦7,500bn; liabilities ₦7,000bn; equity only ₦500bn — leverage of 15×.
The FGN bond book (₦1,850bn) has a duration of 7.5 years.
Most funding is current and savings deposits with a duration of a few months.
Banks earn money by this mismatch — and take risk because of it.

figures.title: How Big a Rate Shock Can the Bank Survive?
points: Each point of higher rates removes roughly ₦124bn of economic equity.
+2 points leaves about ₦251bn; +3 points about ₦127bn.
A rise of about 4 points wipes out equity entirely.
Nigerian 10-year yields rose by almost 5 points between early 2023 and mid-2024.

figures.title: The Hidden Loss Can Exceed Equity
points: Using the 2024 yield curve, the bond book's unrealised loss is about ₦712bn.
That is larger than the bank's ₦500bn equity.
Accounting rules for 'held-to-maturity' bonds can keep this loss off the income statement.
It becomes real only if the bank must sell — for example, in a deposit run.

figures.title: Were Lenders Paid for Inflation?
points: Real 10-year yield = nominal yield − inflation.
It was deeply negative in 2024 (about −16 points).
By end-2025 it was close to zero (about −0.5).
Negative real yields push savers to dollars and real assets; positive ones bring them back to naira bonds.

items: The yield curve's level is the price of money; its slope is the market's view of what comes next.
When yields rise, bond prices fall — long bonds most. Government bonds carry interest-rate risk.
Banks are fragile because they borrow short and lend long with thin equity.
The duration gap turns a rate shock into a naira loss of capital.
Financial conditions reach your firm through the price and quantity of credit.
recap.prework: Read the Thailand: An Imbalance of Payments case. Note the exchange-rate regime, the size of short-term foreign borrowing, and what happened to reserves in 1997.

glossary.def: The annual return on a bond if bought at today's price and held to maturity.
Yields on government debt plotted against maturity.
Short-term yields above long-term yields.
Extra yield investors demand for lending long.
Weighted average time to a bond's cash flows; its rate sensitivity.
Asset duration minus leverage-adjusted liability duration.
Valuing an asset at today's market price.
Accounting label that keeps bond losses off the income statement.
Extra interest a borrower pays above the government yield.
Rules that protect the financial system as a whole.

steps: Tabulate the five yield curves: which are normal and which inverted?

Compute the bank's equity and leverage.
