hook.title: The Bank That Bought Safe Bonds
hook.quote: “We hold government bonds. They never default. What could go wrong?”

concepts.title: What a Yield Curve Shows
concepts.plain: The yield curve plots the interest rate the government pays to borrow for 3 months, 1 year, 10 years and longer. Its level tells you how expensive money is; its slope tells you what markets expect next.
concepts.formula: long yield ≈ average expected short rate + term premium
concepts.example: In 2021 the curve was low and steep (2.5% for 3 months, 12.8% for 10 years). By mid-2024 it was high and inverted (17.5% for 3 months, 21% for 1 year, 18.8% for 10 years).
concepts.why: An inverted curve says markets expect rates to fall later — often because tight policy will slow the economy. It also tells you when to borrow long and when to wait.

concepts.title: When Yields Rise, Bond Prices Fall
concepts.plain: A bond pays fixed coupons. If new bonds pay more, nobody will pay full price for your old, lower-coupon bond — so its price falls until its yield matches the market.
concepts.formula: % price change ≈ − modified duration × change in yield
concepts.example: A 10-year FGN bond with a 13% coupon is worth 100 at a 13% yield, 89.8 at 15%, 77.2 at 18% and 70.2 at 20%.
concepts.why: Duration — roughly the average time until you get your money back — measures sensitivity. The longer the bond, the bigger the fall when rates rise.

concepts.title: The Duration Gap
concepts.plain: The duration gap compares how long the bank's assets are with how long its liabilities are. A positive gap means asset values fall more than liability values when rates rise — so equity shrinks.
concepts.formula: gap = D(assets) − (liabilities ÷ assets) × D(liabilities)
concepts.example: Asset duration 2.38 years, liability duration 0.45 years → gap 1.96 years. A +1 point rise in rates cuts economic equity by about ₦124bn.
concepts.why: The gap turns a rate forecast into a naira number the board understands: how much of our capital a rate shock would destroy.

checks.q: Your pension fund holds a 20-year FGN bond. The CBN signals more rate hikes. What is the most likely effect on the bond's market value?
options: It rises, because higher rates mean higher coupons on the bond you already hold
It falls, and by more than a 2-year bond would
It is unchanged until the bond matures
It falls by the same percentage as a 2-year bond
checks.explain: B. The coupon on an existing bond is fixed, so higher market yields push its price down, and the long duration of a 20-year bond magnifies the fall. C confuses accounting value (if held to maturity) with market value.

checks.q: The case bank's duration gap is 1.96 years and its equity is ₦500bn. A colleague says: 'A 2-point rise in yields is nothing for us.' What is the best reply?
options: Correct — the bonds will pay back at maturity, so there is no loss
A 2-point rise would cut economic equity by about ₦250bn, half our capital
A 2-point rise would wipe out all our equity
We cannot say without the bank's profit figures
checks.explain: B. Change in equity ≈ −1.96 × ₦7,500bn × 0.02 ÷ 1.18 ≈ −₦249bn, about half the ₦500bn. A ignores economic value and liquidity risk. C overstates — that needs about 4 points.

case.title: Could a Nigerian Bank Fall Into the SVB Trap?
case.context: A mid-sized Nigerian bank holds ₦1,850bn of FGN bonds bought around 13%, funded mostly by current and savings deposits. Yields jumped in 2024 as the CBN tightened.
case.question: How much economic value has the bank lost, how big a rate shock could wipe out its equity, and what should the board do?

objectives.body: Compare pegs, managed floats and free floats, and explain the impossible trinity in plain language.

objectives.title: Read the Balance of Payments
objectives.body: Trace where Nigeria's dollars come from and go to, and spot the warning signs of a sudden stop.

objectives.title: Manage Currency Risk
objectives.body: Identify currency mismatch in a business and explain how a weaker naira hits costs, debt and competitiveness.

figures.title: A Decade of Naira Policy
points: 2015–mid-2016: a near-fixed rate around ₦197–199 per dollar.
2016–2023: a managed rate with several official windows, and a wide parallel market.
From June 2023: windows unified; the rate became much more market-determined.
Each switch came after the old regime ran short of dollars.

figures.title: The Premium Measures Rationing
points: The parallel premium averaged about 35% before unification and peaked above 100% in 2016.
Since mid-2024 it has averaged under 3%.
A high premium tells you official dollars are being rationed.
Falling reserves alongside a rising premium is the classic warning of a coming devaluation.

figures.title: Pick Any Two Corners
points: Currency board / monetary union: fixed rate and open capital, but no independent rates (e.g. the euro area, the CFA franc zone).
Capital controls: fixed or managed rate with own policy — at the cost of rationing and parallel markets.
Floating rate: open capital and own policy — the exchange rate does the adjusting.
Nigeria moved from the controls side towards the floating side in 2023–24.

figures.title: Remittances Keep the Account Afloat
points: Remittances (gold) average about US$5.1bn a quarter — a stable dollar source.
Services and income (grey) are a steady drain.
The current account turns negative when oil weakens: about −US$4.6bn in 2020Q2.
Higher oil and a weaker naira restored surpluses in 2023–24.

figures.title: Portfolio Flows Chase the Real Return
points: Foreign portfolio investors come when the real return — interest minus inflation, adjusted for expected depreciation — is attractive.
In our data the correlation between inflows and the real policy rate is 0.45.
These flows can reverse within weeks: a sudden stop.
A central bank that relies on hot money to fund the peg is building a trap.

figures.title: The Dollar Loan That Tripled
points: A firm borrows US$10m in January 2023 to fund naira-earning operations: ₦4.5bn.
By January 2025 the same debt is worth ₦15.4bn.
Nothing changed in the business — only the exchange rate.
Mismatch, not the dollar itself, is the danger: borrow in the currency you earn.

figures.title: Did the Naira Really Get Cheaper?
points: The real rate adjusts the nominal rate for inflation at home and abroad.
From 2016 to 2023 the real index drifted from about 159 to 110: high inflation made the naira overvalued at a fixed rate.
Unification produced a sharp real depreciation (peak about 306 in Feb 2024).
Since then inflation has eroded part of the gain (about 201 by end-2025).

items: The exchange rate is a price set by dollar inflows and outflows.
The impossible trinity: a country must give up one of a fixed rate, free capital or its own policy.
A wide parallel premium means rationing; it usually ends in devaluation.
Hot money can leave fast; remittances are Nigeria's steadiest dollar source.
For firms, the killer is currency mismatch — borrow in the currency you earn.

A currency held at a fixed rate against another.
How much weaker the parallel rate is than the official rate.
A fixed rate, free capital and own monetary policy cannot coexist.
Trade, services, income and transfers with the rest of the world.
Money sent home by citizens working abroad.

An abrupt halt or reversal of capital inflows.
Borrowing in a low-rate currency to invest in a high-rate one.

steps: Compute the parallel premium by year and compare it with reserves.

hook.title: One Dollar, Two Prices
hook.quote: “We buy dollars at the official rate. Our competitor pays the parallel rate. We have a cost advantage — until we don't get any dollars at all.”

concepts.title: What Sets the Exchange Rate?
concepts.plain: An exchange rate is a price: naira per dollar. It is set by who wants dollars (importers, students abroad, investors leaving, people saving in dollars) and who supplies them (oil exporters, remittances, foreign investors coming in, the CBN).
concepts.formula: dollar demand > dollar supply → naira weakens (or reserves fall)
concepts.example: When oil earnings fell in 2015–16 and again in 2020, dollar supply dropped. The CBN either let the naira fall or spent reserves and rationed dollars.
concepts.why: Every forecast of the naira is really a forecast of dollar inflows and outflows. Learn to read those flows and you will rarely be surprised.

concepts.title: The Impossible Trinity
concepts.plain: A country would like three things: a stable exchange rate, free movement of capital, and its own interest-rate policy. It can only have two at a time.
concepts.formula: fixed rate + free capital + own monetary policy = impossible
concepts.example: If the CBN fixes the naira and lets capital move freely, it must set interest rates to defend the peg — it loses control of domestic policy. Nigeria before 2023 kept the peg and its own rates by rationing dollars — a form of capital control.
concepts.why: When a government promises all three, one promise will break. For a business, the question is which one, and when.

concepts.title: Borrow Cheap, Lend Dear — Until the Currency Moves
concepts.plain: In a carry trade, investors borrow in a low-interest currency (dollars) and buy high-yield naira bills. They earn the interest gap — as long as the naira does not fall by more than that gap.
concepts.formula: carry return ≈ naira yield − dollar yield − naira depreciation
concepts.example: A 20% naira bill against a 5% dollar cost earns about 15% — but a 40% devaluation turns that into a large loss.
concepts.why: When carry investors all head for the exit at once, the naira falls fast and reserves drain. Watch their positioning, not just the interest rate.

checks.q: A country fixes its currency, allows investors to move money freely, and wants to cut interest rates to boost growth. What is most likely to happen?
options: Growth rises and the peg holds
Investors move money out to earn higher returns abroad, reserves fall, and the peg comes under pressure
Inflation falls automatically
Nothing changes because the rate is fixed
checks.explain: B. With open capital, lower domestic rates push money out. To hold the peg the central bank must sell reserves — which cannot last. This is exactly the impossible trinity at work.

checks.q: Your company borrowed US$10m in January 2023 at 8% a year instead of ₦4.5bn at 18%. Using the stylised rates, what is the main lesson two years later?
options: The dollar loan was cheaper because 8% < 18%
The naira value of the dollar debt rose from about ₦4.5bn to ₦15.4bn, wiping out the interest saving many times over
The two loans cost the same
Exchange rates don't matter for debt
checks.explain: B. The interest gap saved about 10 points a year, but the naira fell by roughly 70% against the dollar, more than tripling the naira value of the principal. Always include expected depreciation.

case.question: Why did the old system break, who gained and lost from unification, and what should a Nigerian firm do differently now?

figures.title: Who Nigeria Trades With
points: Exports go mainly to oil buyers: the United States, India and European refiners.
Imports come overwhelmingly from China: machinery, phones, textiles, inputs.
Total trade in this stylised year is about $31bn; trade with African partners is only 7.6% of it.
That low African share is the gap AfCFTA is meant to close.

figures.title: Export Concentration: Oil Still Dominates
points: Oil and gas make up about 74% of exports in these data.
When oil prices or output fall, export earnings — and dollars for importers — fall with them.
Non-oil exports are about $3.5bn; Africa already takes $849m of them, second only to Asia.
Manufactured and processed goods are more likely to sell in Africa than in Europe.

figures.title: Size Pulls, Distance Pushes
points: Each bubble is a partner; bigger bubble = bigger economy.
Distant giants (China, the US) still trade heavily with Nigeria because of their size.
Neighbours like Benin and Ghana trade a lot for their size — they are very close.
Small, landlocked and distant partners such as Chad trade very little.

figures.title: What Drives Nigeria's Trade?
points: GDP elasticity ≈ 0.98; distance elasticity ≈ −1.08.
A shared language goes with about 73% more trade.
Landlocked partners trade about 52% less — every border and truck adds cost.
Four variables explain 89% of the variation (R² = 0.89).

figures.title: Where Is Trade Below What Gravity Predicts?
points: A ratio below 1 means Nigeria trades less than size and distance suggest.
Côte d'Ivoire (0.72×), Egypt and Ghana sit below the line — potential room to grow.
South Africa (1.84×) and Cameroon (1.66×) already trade more than predicted.
Missing trade is a clue, not a verdict: check non-tariff barriers, payments and competition first.

figures.title: What Removing Tariffs Could Do
points: Trade with African partners: about $2.4bn today in these data.
If average tariffs fell from 9% to zero and trade responds with an elasticity of 4, trade rises about 41% to $3.4bn.
The elasticity is uncertain — estimates often range from 3 to 6 — so treat this as a range, not a forecast.
Poor roads, slow borders, checkpoints and payment frictions can cost more than the tariff itself.

figures.title: One Supplier Country, One Point of Failure
points: China supplies about 64% of Nigeria's imports in these data.
The Herfindahl–Hirschman Index (sum of squared shares) is 4,178 — above 2,500 is commonly treated as highly concentrated.
The top three sources supply 76% of imports.
A port closure, export ban or freight spike in one place can stop Nigerian factories.

items: Countries — and firms — gain by specialising in their comparative advantage.
Trade follows gravity: big and close partners matter most; use it to spot missing trade.
AfCFTA cuts tariffs, but logistics, rules of origin, payments and FX decide whether you can compete.
Measure supplier concentration; diversify, stock, localise and map deeper tiers.
Industrial policy works best with discipline, competition and an exit date.
recap.prework: Read Stern, The Economics of Climate Change (summary chapters) and skim the KPMG / IFRS Foundation guide on ISSB and TCFD. List your company's three largest sources of emissions.

What you give up to produce or buy something.

% change in one thing for a 1% change in another.
The African Continental Free Trade Area.

Sum of squared shares; measures concentration.
Moving supply chains to politically aligned countries.

steps: Rank partners by total trade and compute Africa's share.
Fit the gravity model: log trade on log GDP, log distance, language and landlocked.
Compare actual vs predicted trade for each African partner.

hook.title: A Market of 1.3 Billion People Next Door
hook.quote: “AfCFTA opens a continent. Let's export everywhere next year.”

concepts.title: Everyone Gains From Doing What They Do Relatively Best
concepts.plain: A country gains from trade by producing what it gives up least to make — its comparative advantage — and buying the rest. Even a country that is better at everything gains by specialising.
concepts.formula: opportunity cost of X = output of Y given up ÷ extra output of X
concepts.example: If a Nigerian worker can make 10 bags of cement or 2 phones a day, and a Chinese worker 12 bags or 6 phones, Nigeria gives up 0.2 phones per bag; China gives up 0.5. Nigeria has the comparative advantage in cement, China in phones — even though China is better at both.
concepts.why: Comparative advantage is not fixed. Nigeria moved from importing most of its cement to producing almost all of it once investment, gas and scale came together. Your firm's export opportunity lies where your cost relative to rivals is lowest.

concepts.title: Trade Behaves Like Gravity
concepts.plain: Countries trade more with partners that are big and close, and less with those that are small and far — just as gravity pulls more strongly between heavy, nearby objects. Shared language, borders and history add to the pull; being landlocked subtracts.
concepts.formula: log(trade) = a + b₁·log(GDP) + b₂·log(distance) + extras
concepts.example: In our data b₁ = 0.98 and b₂ = −1.08: a partner 10% bigger trades about 10% more with Nigeria; one 10% further away trades about 11% less.
concepts.why: Gravity is the most reliable model in international economics. It tells you what trade should be with each market — so you can spot where trade is missing and where the opportunity is real.

concepts.title: The Herfindahl–Hirschman Index
concepts.plain: Square each supplier's percentage share and add them up. One supplier = 10,000. Many small suppliers = close to zero. The higher the number, the more your supply depends on a few sources.
concepts.formula: HHI = s₁² + s₂² + … + sₙ²   (shares in %)
concepts.example: 64% from China, 7% from Germany, 5% from the US and many small sources → HHI ≈ 4,178. Splitting China's share across two countries of 32% each would roughly halve that contribution.
concepts.why: Run this on your own purchase ledger by country and by supplier. An HHI above 2,500 on a critical input is a board-level risk.

checks.q: The gravity model says Nigeria trades only 0.72 times the predicted amount with Côte d'Ivoire. What is the best interpretation for an exporter?
options: Ivorians do not like Nigerian products
There may be unexploited potential — investigate the barriers (language, logistics, payments, rules) before investing
The model is wrong and should be ignored
Côte d'Ivoire is too far away to matter
checks.explain: B. 'Missing trade' signals possible potential relative to size and distance. The reason could be language (French), currency (CFA franc), logistics or rules — each is fixable at a cost. A and D are not supported; C throws away a useful benchmark.

checks.q: Your firm imports 70% of a critical packaging input from one country. Interest rates are 27%. Which response is most sensible first?
options: Triple inventory immediately
Qualify a second supplier in another country and map who your current supplier depends on
Stop importing and wait for local supply to appear
Do nothing — diversification is too expensive
checks.explain: B. Qualifying a second source and mapping the deeper tiers reduce concentration without the large cash cost of tripling stock at 27% interest (A). C risks stopping production; D ignores a board-level risk.

case.title: AfCFTA and a Nigerian Manufacturer
case.context: A Lagos packaged-food manufacturer sells only in Nigeria. AfCFTA lowers tariffs on most goods traded between member states, and the board wants an export plan. Most of its packaging and machinery are imported.
case.question: Which African markets should it enter first — and how should it make its supply chain shock-proof before it grows?
case.data: ng_trade_partners.csv — Nigeria's exports and imports with 30 partners, plus partner GDP, distance, language, AfCFTA membership and tariffs. *Stylised teaching data.*

objectives.title: Explain Carbon Pricing
objectives.body: Explain why emissions are an externality, and how carbon taxes, trading schemes and border adjustments put a price on them.

objectives.title: Size the Exposure
objectives.body: Turn emissions and a carbon price into a naira cost, and compare it with EBITDA by sector and by firm.

objectives.title: Plan the Response
objectives.body: Use pass-through, abatement and disclosure to build a credible transition plan for a Nigerian business.

figures.title: Carbon Intensity Differs Enormously by Sector
points: Power generation (0.98) and cement (0.81) emit most per ₦1 million of revenue.
Steel (0.77) and upstream oil & gas (0.57) follow.
Banking (0.01) and telecoms (0.08) emit very little directly — but they lend to and serve the heavy emitters.
Intensity, not total emissions, tells you how a carbon price hits margins.

figures.title: The Carbon Bill as a Share of EBITDA
points: At US$50/t: steel loses about 33% of EBITDA, power 25%, cement 16%.
At US$100/t: steel 66%, power 50%, cement 32%.
Banking, telecoms and solar lose under 3% even at US$100.
These are worst cases: no pass-through and no abatement.

figures.title: Who Is Really Exposed?
points: High intensity and a thin margin is the danger zone.
9 of 40 firms would lose more than a fifth of EBITDA at US$50/t.
Firms within one sector differ — the best cement plant is far cleaner than the worst.
Investors will reward the clean firms within dirty sectors.

figures.title: Cement vs Solar as the Carbon Price Rises
points: Cement EBITDA falls steadily as the price rises — about 16% lower at US$50.
Solar is almost unaffected — and may gain if it sells power to emitters.
The same policy moves value from high-carbon to low-carbon businesses.
This is what investors mean by transition risk.

figures.title: Big Slice of EU Sales, Small Slice of Profit
points: Cement and steel are the Nigerian sectors most directly covered.
The charge equals 8–14% of EU export revenue for these firms.
Because EU sales are a small share of total sales, the hit to group EBITDA is smaller.
But the EU price is the benchmark other markets may follow.

figures.title: Can Cement Pass the Cost On?
points: Passing the bill on in prices protects margin — if customers stay.
With few substitutes (elasticity −0.3), full pass-through leaves EBITDA only about 2% lower.
If imports compete (elasticity −1.5), lost volume still costs about 12% of EBITDA.
Session 2's elasticity is the key to any carbon strategy.

figures.title: Cut the Cheap Tonnes First
points: A marginal abatement cost curve ranks options by cost per tonne saved.
Waste-heat recovery and clinker substitution save money even with no carbon price.
Below a US$50 price, about 295 of 495 thousand tonnes can be cut profitably.
Carbon capture is the expensive last resort.

figures.title: Only a Minority Report Today
points: About 30% of the stylised firms publish TCFD-style reports.
Disclosure is highest in telecoms, solar and steel (2 of 3 firms each).
None of the upstream oil & gas firms disclose — exactly where investors most need data.
Early movers gain credibility with lenders and DFIs.

items: Emissions are an externality; a carbon price makes the emitter pay.
Exposure depends on intensity and margins, not on total emissions alone.
CBAM brings EU carbon prices to Nigerian cement and steel exports.
Pass-through depends on elasticity; abatement should start with the cheapest tonnes.
Disclosure under TCFD/ISSB is becoming the price of access to capital.
recap.prework: Read India: Liberalise in the Face of Crisis? Note the warning signs before 1991 and how policymakers responded. Bring one indicator you would watch to judge a country's risk.

glossary.def: A cost or benefit that falls on people outside the transaction.
A charge per tonne of CO₂ emitted, via a tax or permits.
Emissions trading system: a cap on emissions with tradable permits.
The EU's charge on embedded carbon in certain imports.
Direct emissions / emissions from purchased electricity.
Emissions per unit of output or revenue.
Losses from policy, technology and market shifts to low carbon.
Losses from floods, heat, drought and storms.
An asset that loses value early because of the transition.
Marginal abatement cost curve: emission cuts ranked by cost per tonne.

lab.title: Lab: Carbon Stress Test for Your Sector
steps: Compute each firm's total emissions (scope 1 + 2) and intensity per ₦1 million of revenue.
Compute the carbon bill at US$25, 50 and 100 a tonne (₦1,500/US$).
Express it as a % of EBITDA by sector and rank the sectors.
List the ten most exposed firms and check whether they disclose.
Rerun with a different exchange rate and with a 30% abatement.
lab.deliver: three sentences for a cement board: our exposure, what customers will bear, and our first two actions.

hook.title: Same Price, Different Fates
hook.quote: “Carbon pricing is a European problem. We sell in Nigeria.”

concepts.title: Emissions Are an Externality
concepts.plain: When a kiln or generator emits CO₂, the damage — floods, heat, crop losses — falls on other people, mostly in the future. The emitter does not pay, so the market produces too much pollution.
concepts.formula: social cost = private cost + damage to others
concepts.example: Nigeria's 2022 floods displaced over a million people. No cement plant, power station or car owner paid for its share of the emissions that make such events more likely.
concepts.why: When governments correct an externality, costs that were hidden on someone else's books move on to yours. Planning for that is risk management, not politics.

concepts.title: The EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism
concepts.plain: CBAM makes EU importers pay for the carbon embedded in certain goods — cement, iron and steel, aluminium, fertilisers, electricity and hydrogen — at roughly the EU carbon price, minus any carbon price already paid where the goods were made.
concepts.formula: CBAM charge ≈ embedded tonnes × (EU price − carbon price paid at home)
concepts.example: For the stylised cement and steel exporters, an EU price of US$80/t costs about 8–14% of EU export revenue — but only 2–11% of total EBITDA, because most sales are domestic.
concepts.why: Reporting started in October 2023; payment obligations begin for imports from 2026. Exporters that measure and cut their emissions keep their EU customers.

checks.q: At US$50 a tonne, the stylised cement sector's carbon bill is about ₦252bn, or 16% of its EBITDA. A director says: 'That is only 6% of revenue — not a big deal.' What is the best reply?
options: Agreed — what matters is revenue
The relevant comparison is profit: losing a sixth of EBITDA, before any pass-through, is material for valuation and debt covenants
The bill is zero because Nigeria has no carbon price
Carbon costs are always passed on fully to customers
checks.explain: B. A cost of 6% of revenue is 16% of EBITDA, and more of net profit. C ignores the scenario purpose and CBAM on exports. D depends on competition and demand elasticity — see the next part.

checks.q: A cement firm can cut 110 thousand tonnes of CO₂ by substituting clinker, at a cost of –US$10 a tonne (it saves money). Why might it not have done so already?
options: Because the option saves money, it must already have been done
Upfront capital, management attention, technical risk or customer acceptance can block profitable cuts — a carbon price or disclosure pressure tips the balance
Abatement only makes sense when the carbon price is above US$100
Clinker substitution increases emissions
checks.explain: B. Negative-cost options often stay undone because of financing constraints, habit or perceived risk. A carbon price raises their payoff further; disclosure makes inaction visible. C misreads the curve.

case.title: Cement vs Solar Under a Carbon Price
case.context: A board is comparing two holdings: a cement producer with coal- and gas-fired kilns and a solar installer. Both are profitable today.
case.question: If a carbon price of US$25, US$50 or US$100 a tonne applied, how much EBITDA would each lose — and what can management do about it?
case.data: firm_carbon_exposure.csv — 40 fictional Nigerian listed firms in 9 sectors: revenue, EBITDA, scope 1 and 2 emissions, EU export share, TCFD disclosure. *Stylised teaching data.* We assume ₦1,500 per US$.
case.decision: A carbon stress test by sector and firm, plus a response plan: pass-through, abatement and disclosure.

objectives.title: Score Country Risk
objectives.body: Build a transparent country-risk score from political, policy, external, fiscal and banking indicators.

objectives.title: Plan with Scenarios
objectives.body: Replace a single forecast with a few plausible scenarios, probabilities and signposts.

objectives.title: Stress-Test a Plan
objectives.body: Find the shocks that hurt a business plan most, and decide what to do about them in advance.

figures.title: Eight Markets at a Glance
points: Rows are markets, columns indicators; the number is the raw value, the colour its relative risk.
Morocco and Côte d'Ivoire are green across most columns.
Nigeria is red on governance and inflation, but green on reserves and debt.
Egypt and Ethiopia are red on debt, spreads and FX.

figures.title: Equal Weights: Who Is Riskiest?
points: Averaging the four pillars equally and rescaling to 0–100.
Morocco (0) and Côte d'Ivoire (8) are the safest in this group.
Nigeria scores 66, behind Ethiopia (71) and Egypt (100).
A score is relative to this group, not an absolute probability of default.

figures.title: Change the Weights, Change the Answer
points: A lender cares most about external and fiscal risk: Nigeria rises to 3rd safest thanks to reserves and moderate debt.
An investor cares most about macro and policy: Nigeria becomes the riskiest of the eight.
The ends of the table are stable; the middle is fragile.
Always report the weights — and test whether your decision changes if they change.

figures.title: Big Markets Are Not Always Safe Markets
points: Vertical axis: market size in five years (population grown at the real growth rate).
Nigeria, Ethiopia and Egypt are the big prizes — and among the riskiest.
Morocco and Côte d'Ivoire are safer but smaller.
Strategy is choosing where on this map your firm can earn a premium for the risk it takes.

figures.title: The Plan's EBITDA Under Three Worlds
points: Today's EBITDA: ₦18bn.
Reform: ₦18.4bn. Muddle through: ₦11.2bn. Relapse: a loss of ₦5.9bn.
Probability-weighted EBITDA: ₦10.3bn — well below today.
The relapse case decides how much debt and fixed cost the plan can carry.

figures.title: Which Shock Hurts Most?
points: Starting from 'muddle through' (₦11.2bn), apply one shock at a time.
Losing 30 points of pricing power costs about ₦6.3bn — the biggest hit.
A further 30% naira fall costs about ₦4.2bn.
Rates and demand matter less for this firm — so focus hedging and pricing strategy there.

figures.title: Nigeria Today: Green, Amber or Red?
points: Reserves at 7 months of imports: green.
Inflation (24%), Eurobond spread (5.5%), FX depreciation (24%) and debt (52% of GDP): amber.
No indicator is red — consistent with 'muddle through'.
Review monthly with the dashboard from Session 1.

items: Country risk has several families: macro, external, fiscal, political and banking.
Put indicators on one scale (z-scores) and make the weights explicit.
Rankings can flip with the weights — test before you decide.
Plan with three scenarios and a probability-weighted outcome, not one forecast.
Agree signposts and triggers in advance so action is fast.
recap.prework: Read Acharya, Almeida, Amihud & Liu, 'Corporate Resiliency and the Choice Between Financial and Operational Hedging' (NBER). Note one example of an operational hedge in your own company.

glossary.def: The chance that conditions in a country hurt an investment or business.
The risk of not being able to convert or move money out.
Distance from the group average, in standard deviations.
A group of related indicators combined into one sub-score.
How much each pillar counts in the final score.
A coherent, plausible story about the future.
Scenarios with probabilities and outcomes laid out together.
An indicator showing which scenario is unfolding.
A pre-agreed level at which management acts.
Measuring the impact of a severe but plausible shock.

lab.title: Lab: Rank Eight Markets, Stress-Test Nigeria
steps: Convert the nine indicators into risk z-scores (flip the sign where high is good).
Average them into four pillars.
Rank the markets under equal, lender and investor weights.
Compute the plan's probability-weighted EBITDA across three scenarios.
Choose three signposts and the trigger levels that would change your plan.
lab.deliver: a ranked shortlist with your weights stated, and a one-paragraph scenario note for the Nigeria plan.

hook.title: Where Should We Expand Next?
hook.quote: “Nigeria is our biggest market, so it must be our best market.”

concepts.title: Turning Different Indicators into One Score
concepts.plain: Inflation is in %, reserves in months and governance on a −2.5 to +2.5 scale. To combine them, express each as a z-score: how far a country is from the group average, in standard deviations. Flip the sign where high is good, so higher always means riskier.
concepts.formula: z = (value − group average) ÷ standard deviation
concepts.example: Nigeria's political-stability score (−1.9) is well below the group average, giving a high risk z-score. Its reserves (7 months) are above average, giving a low one.
concepts.why: Writing the method down makes your judgement auditable. Colleagues can argue about the weights instead of arguing about gut feel.

concepts.title: Signposts and Triggers
concepts.plain: A signpost is an indicator that tells you which scenario is unfolding. A trigger is the level at which you act — agreed in advance, so the decision is not made in panic.
concepts.formula: signpost crosses trigger → pre-agreed action
concepts.example: If 12-month naira depreciation passes 30% (red), switch to the relapse playbook: raise prices faster, cut dollar inventory, delay capex.
concepts.why: Most firms see the warning signs and still react late. Pre-agreed triggers turn foresight into action.

checks.q: A colleague's spreadsheet ranks Nigeria 3rd safest of eight markets; yours ranks it 8th. Both use the same data. What is the most likely explanation?
options: One of you made an arithmetic error
You used different weights: hers stresses reserves and debt, yours stresses inflation and governance
Nigeria's data are unreliable
Country risk cannot be measured
checks.explain: B. With these data, a lender-style weighting puts Nigeria 3rd and an investor-style weighting puts it 8th. The disagreement is about priorities — which is a useful conversation once it is made explicit.

checks.q: The stress test shows that losing pricing power hurts the Nigeria plan more than a further 30% naira fall. Which action follows most directly?
options: Buy more dollar forwards
Invest in brand strength, product mix and pricing processes so price increases stick
Exit Nigeria
Ignore the result because the naira is the bigger headline risk
checks.explain: B. The tornado shows where the plan is most fragile. Protecting pricing power (brand, mix, route to market) addresses the largest exposure; hedging (Session 15) addresses the second.

case.title: Eight Markets, One Expansion Budget
case.context: A Lagos-based consumer-goods group will expand into one more African market and must also defend its Nigerian business, which earns ₦18bn EBITDA on ₦120bn revenue with 45% of costs imported.
case.question: How do the eight candidate markets rank on risk, does the ranking survive different weightings, and how badly could the Nigeria plan be hit next year?
case.data: country_risk_panel.csv — eight African markets × ten indicators: growth, inflation, debt, reserves, current account, governance, FX depreciation, Eurobond spreads. *Stylised teaching data.* Plan model assumptions are stated on each chart.
case.decision: A ranked shortlist with the weighting stated openly, a three-scenario plan for Nigeria, and a signpost board that tells management when to switch plans.

objectives.title: Measure Macro Exposure
objectives.body: Trace how the exchange rate, commodity prices and interest rates flow into revenue, costs and margin.

objectives.title: Choose the Right Hedge
objectives.body: Compare natural, operational and financial hedges, and pick a sensible hedge ratio — not automatically 100%.

objectives.title: Build Resilience
objectives.body: Use a risk heatmap, real options and leading indicators to prepare before the shock arrives.

figures.title: Wheat in Dollars, Dollars in Naira
points: By December 2025 the naira cost of a tonne of wheat was about five times its 2019 level (index 505).
The dollar price of wheat ended only 6% above 2019, after a spike in 2022.
The exchange rate index reached 474: the naira did most of the damage.
Lesson: the miller's real exposure is to the naira, not to wheat.

figures.title: The Exchange Rate Did the Damage
points: Wheat price in US$: +9 log-points.
Naira per US$: +160 log-points.
Together: naira wheat cost up 438% between the 2019 and 2025 averages.
The currency explains 95% of the increase.

figures.title: Costs Move First, Prices Follow
points: Average gross margin 2019–2025: 21.3%.
Each devaluation hit the margin before flour prices could follow.
Worst months: −0.1% in February 2024, 8.4% in July 2023 and 10.0% in January 2024.
Margins recovered as prices caught up — a natural hedge, but a slow one.

figures.title: A Sensitivity 'Tornado'
points: Starting point: 2025 average margin of 25.2%.
A 20% weaker naira, or 20% dearer wheat, each cuts the margin by 15 points.
Both together: −32.9 points — the miller would make a loss.
Other costs matter far less (±2 points). Spend management time where the tornado is widest.

figures.title: Hedging 0%, 50% or 100% of Next Quarter's Dollars
points: Each month the miller can lock in the rate for wheat it will pay for in three months.
Unhedged, the margin fell to −0.1% in the 2024 devaluation.
Fully hedged, the margin jumped in the same months — prices rose while costs were locked.
In calm years hedging cost margin: average 21.8% unhedged vs 20.4% fully hedged.

figures.title: Why 100% Is Not the Safest Hedge
points: 50% hedged had the lowest volatility: 3.5 points vs 4.9 unhedged and 6.5 fully hedged.
Its worst month was 12.7%, against −0.1% unhedged.
100% over-hedged: flour prices already follow the naira, so a full hedge creates a new mismatch.
The right hedge ratio covers the exposure that your prices cannot pass on.

figures.title: The Macro-Risk Heatmap
points: Score each risk for likelihood and impact (1–5); the product ranks them.
Naira devaluation (4 × 5 = 20) and wheat spikes (3 × 4 = 12) lead.
Impact scores come from the sensitivity tornado, not gut feel.
Review the map every quarter — scores change as signposts move.

figures.title: Signals That Warn Before the Shock
points: When the parallel premium was above 30%, the naira fell on average 23.4% over the next six months.
When it was below 30%, the average was 7.0%.
The correlation is moderate (r = 0.43): a warning light, not a forecast.
Raise the hedge ratio, or stock up, when several warning lights turn on together.

items: Measure exposure first: decompose costs into commodity and currency parts.
For Nigerian importers, the exchange rate usually dominates.
Hedge the exposure your prices cannot pass on — 100% can over-hedge.
Forward cover costs roughly the interest-rate gap; know when it is worth paying.
Build operational resilience and watch leading indicators with pre-agreed triggers.
recap.prework: Prepare for the capstone: choose your industry, draft the one-page macro memo to your board using the template on the course site, and bring three charts as evidence.

glossary.def: A known foreign-currency payment or receipt on a future date.
Revaluation of foreign-currency assets and debts on the balance sheet.
Long-run effect of macro changes on competitiveness and demand.
An offsetting exposure inside the business, e.g. dollar revenue against dollar costs.
An agreement today on the rate for a future currency exchange.
How much weaker the forward rate is than spot; set by the rate gap.
Share of an exposure covered by a hedge.
The right to change course later: delay, expand, switch or exit.
How much an outcome moves when one input changes.
A signal that tends to move before the outcome you care about.

lab.title: Lab: A Hedging Plan for the Miller
steps: Map the exposure: which costs are in dollars, and how did the margin behave?
Decompose the rise in naira wheat cost into wheat and exchange-rate parts.
Build a 3-month forward price from the interest-rate gap.
Simulate hedge ratios of 0, 25, 50, 75 and 100% and compare average, volatility and worst month.
Run the sensitivity test and score your own company's top five risks.

hook.title: Profitable — Until the Naira Moved
hook.quote: “We buy wheat in dollars and sell bread flour in naira. In February 2024 our gross margin was zero.”

concepts.title: How Much Came From Each Source?
concepts.plain: A naira cost of an imported input is dollar price × exchange rate. In logs, the two parts simply add up, so you can split any rise into a 'commodity' part and a 'currency' part.
concepts.formula: Δln(₦ cost) = Δln(US$ price) + Δln(₦ per US$)
concepts.example: 2019 → 2025 averages: wheat +9 log-points, naira +160 log-points. Total rise 438%, of which the exchange rate explains 95%.
concepts.why: It tells you which hedge matters. Buying wheat futures in Chicago would have done little; managing the naira exposure was everything.

concepts.title: What a Naira Forward Should Cost
concepts.plain: A forward fixes today the rate at which you will buy dollars later. Banks price it so nobody can earn a free profit: the naira forward is weaker than spot by roughly the interest-rate gap between naira and dollars.
concepts.formula: Forward ≈ Spot × (1 + (i₦ − i$) × months ÷ 12)
concepts.example: December 2025: spot ₦1,454, MPR 27%, US rate about 3.75% → 3-month forward ≈ ₦1,539, a premium of 5.8% a quarter.
concepts.why: Hedging is not free: at a 27% naira rate, rolling three-month cover costs over 20% a year in calm times. It pays off only when the naira falls by more than the premium.

concepts.title: Flexibility Is a Hedge Too
concepts.plain: A real option is the right, but not the obligation, to change course later — like having a second supplier ready, or a plant that can switch inputs. It costs something today and pays off when the world turns against you.
concepts.formula: Value of flexibility = value with the option − value without it
concepts.example: Testing a cassava-wheat blend costs ₦ today. If the naira falls 20%, switching 10% of wheat to local cassava cuts the dollar bill exactly when it hurts most.
concepts.why: Options to delay, expand, switch or exit are often cheaper and longer-lasting than financial contracts, which may not exist for long tenors in naira.

checks.q: The miller's naira wheat cost rose 438% between 2019 and 2025. Wheat in dollars rose about 9%. Which hedge would have helped most?
options: Buying wheat futures to fix the dollar price
Fixing the naira cost of dollars in advance (FX forwards) and passing costs on faster
Borrowing more in dollars at low rates
Holding larger stocks of flour
checks.explain: B. The currency explained 95% of the rise, so FX hedging and faster price pass-through matter most. A addresses the small part. C adds currency risk. D protects supply but not cost.

checks.q: The miller's prices follow the naira with a lag of a few months. The board asks to hedge 100% of FX for the next year. What is the best response?
options: Agree — full hedging removes all risk
Hedge only the part of the exposure that prices cannot pass on, over the lag period — roughly half for a few months — and review quarterly
Refuse all hedging — the naira forward premium is too high
Hedge 100% but for five years to save on fees
checks.explain: B. Because prices already pass on costs with a lag, a full hedge over-hedges and adds a new mismatch, as the simulation showed. C ignores real devaluation risk; D locks in a long, costly and probably unavailable contract.

case.context: A Lagos flour miller imports all its wheat, paid in US dollars about three months after ordering. It sells flour to bakers and noodle makers in naira, and can raise prices only gradually.
case.question: Which macro risks matter most, how much of its dollar cost should it hedge, and what else should it do to protect its margin?

figures.title: Worked Example: The Cement Industry
points: Volumes: +10.3% over the last 12 months.
Price per bag: about ₦9,079.
Real policy rate: +10.6 points — expensive mortgages and developer credit.
PMI 52.9: activity expanding. Evidence for a cautious 'grow, but protect margin' memo.

figures.title: Don't Be Fooled by Naira Prices
points: The price of a bag of cement rose +345% in naira since 2015.
Adjusted for inflation, it fell about 24%.
A memo that celebrates naira price growth without deflating it misleads the board.
Session 1's first lesson is still the most important one.

figures.title: Sixteen Sessions, One Logic
points: Part I: how markets set prices and quantities, and where they fail.
Part II: how the whole economy moves — inflation, output, money, budgets, banks.
Part III: how Nigeria connects to the world — currency, capital and trade.
Part IV: how a firm turns all of it into strategy — climate, country risk, hedging, the board memo.

figures.title: One Shock, Four Panels
points: June 2023: FX unification and petrol subsidy removal.
The naira moved from about ₦463 to a peak near ₦1,657 per dollar.
Inflation peaked near 34.5%; the CBN raised its rate from 11.5% (early 2022) to 27.5%.
A flour miller's gross margin fell to about zero at the worst point — policy reaches the P&L within months.

figures.title: The Global Tide and Nigeria's Rate
points: The US Fed's rate moves capital worldwide; emerging markets must pay a premium to keep it.
In late 2025 the CBN's rate was about 23 points above the Fed's.
Part of that gap is Nigerian inflation; part is the risk premium investors demand.
When the Fed cuts, pressure on the naira usually eases — one signpost for your memo.

figures.title: Three Scenarios for 2026
points: Upside (reforms stick, oil firm): naira about ₦1,386, inflation about 13% by end-2026.
Base (gradual disinflation): about ₦1,600 and 15%.
Downside (oil slump, renewed FX pressure): about ₦2,073 and 24%.
These are teaching scenarios, not forecasts — build your own for the memo.

items: Think in incentives, margins and opportunity cost — and always separate real from nominal.
Prices, inflation, rates and the naira are linked: one shock travels through all of them.
Nigeria is an open economy: oil, the Fed and capital flows shape what the CBN can do.
Plan with scenarios, signposts and hedges, not a single forecast.
Tell the board what to do, why, and what would change your mind.

checks.q: Practice: the Fed cuts rates by 1 point while Nigerian inflation is stable. Which chain is most likely for a Lagos importer?
options: Higher naira borrowing costs immediately
Capital flows toward emerging markets, easing pressure on the naira and the cost of imported inputs
No effect, because the Fed only affects the US
Higher Nigerian inflation
checks.explain: B. Lower US rates make naira assets relatively more attractive (carry), supporting the naira. The importer's dollar costs in naira fall or stabilise. The effect is not guaranteed — oil and domestic policy matter too.

checks.q: Practice: a board member says 'our dollar loan at 7% is cheaper than a naira loan at 22%'. What do you check first?
options: Nothing — 7% is lower
The expected depreciation of the naira and whether our revenues are in naira (currency mismatch)
The Fed's balance sheet
The CPI rebasing
checks.explain: B. The true cost of the dollar loan is roughly 7% plus expected naira depreciation. With naira revenues, a large devaluation can make it far dearer (Session 11).
